questions.question: A layer declares index_encoding 1 and entry_count = 70,000. What must extent_length equal — give the exact u64 value in hexadecimal?

questions.why_it_matters: Applies the §7.4 extent_length formula (entry_count × 20 + ⌈entry_count/2^16⌉ × 4) to a concrete entry_count that crosses one segment boundary, so both terms of the formula are live.

questions.question: Per §6.4's writer guidance, if a writer wants to guarantee that a single 64 KiB suffix fetch always captures the trailer and the directory together, what is the maximum dir_length (in bytes) it should keep, assuming the worst-case pre-trailer pad the commit protocol allows?
questions.answer_form: an integer byte count
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the 65,536-byte discovery-window budget with the commit protocol's pad-to-next-64-byte-boundary rule to derive a bound neither section states directly.

questions.question: Per §2.3's reach rule (R-CNF-13), exactly which rows of §21.2's file-scope register reach (apply to) a file declaring a format major other than 1, and how many total instances is that (counting each row's distinct instances separately, e.g. F1's two)?
questions.answer_form: a list of row labels plus a total instance count
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the carve-out that only conditions asserting an invariant R-CNT-24 fixes in every format major 'reach' a file of another declared major — a quantified exception a rewording easily loses or miscounts.

questions.question: A file's live trailer currently has committed_file_length = 1,048,576. The writer now performs its next commit. What is the minimum legal value (in hexadecimal) that this commit's new committed_file_length may take?
questions.answer_form: a hex u64 value
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the commit protocol's 'at least 128 bytes more' derivation with the trailer rule that committed_file_length must be a multiple of 64, applied to a concrete starting value.

questions.question: A planar layer declares dimensions, in order, (y, x) with extents (1000, 2049) and tile extents (256, 256), and 3 channels. What is the disk ordinal of the tile covering tile coordinates (y = 3, x = 7) for channel index 1 (0-based)?
questions.answer_form: a single integer
questions.why_it_matters: Requires computing grid counts from extents/tile-extents, the spatial ordinal under row-major linearization, and then the planar disk-ordinal formula c·N+s — three combined steps, none of which is read off a table.

questions.question: An interleaved layer declares channels, in order, u (uint32), v (int16), w (bool), and has tile extents (4, 4). What is the byte offset, within one tile's decoded image, of channel w's value at in-tile coordinates (2, 3)?
questions.answer_form: a single integer byte offset
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the in-tile ordinal formula with the interleaved byte-offset formula (sample stride and per-channel in-sample offset), where getting channel order or stride wrong changes the answer.

questions.question: A planar bool channel declares fill = true (the byte 0x01). One of its addressed, fully-stored tiles has exactly P = 20 sample positions, every one of them a real (non-edge-padding) array position, and every one of those 20 real values is false. What are the tile's three decoded bytes, in hexadecimal, in stored order?
questions.answer_form: three hex bytes in order
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the distinction between padding positions (array-level, only at edge tiles) and pad bits (packing-level, arising whenever P isn't a multiple of 8 regardless of edge status) — an interior, fully-real tile still has pad bits here, and they must carry the fill bit, not zero.

questions.question: A planar layer has one uint64 channel, and every addressed tile has P = 300,000,000 sample positions. The layer declares codec 4 (lz4). Is this declaration conforming? If not, name the outcome class and the owning scope, and state whether a reader can detect the violation from the layer's declarations alone, without fetching any tile payload.
questions.answer_form: a verdict plus outcome-class name plus scope, plus yes/no on declaration-only detectability
questions.why_it_matters: Requires computing a planar channel's decoded size (P × element size) and comparing it against the 0x7E000000 lz4 cap, then applying the 'largest channel plane governs' quantifier and the rule that this is checkable from declarations alone.

questions.question: A single layer declares a dimension named z and, separately, a channel also named z. Is this a conforming layer under R-ENC-15? If it is permitted, name the specific textual reason in one phrase.
questions.answer_form: a verdict plus a short phrase naming the reason
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the explicit carve-out that dimension names and channel names are separate namespaces within one layer — easy to lose in a rewording that states name-uniqueness as a single undifferentiated rule.

questions.question: A planar layer has spatial-tile count N = 100,000 and channel count C = 4. A reader requests all 4 channels at spatial ordinal s = 50,000. Not counting the single shared crc_of_crc_array check, how many distinct index segments must the reader verify at minimum to serve this request?
questions.answer_form: a single integer
questions.why_it_matters: Requires computing four disk ordinals (c·N+s for c=0..3), mapping each to its segment index (floor(ordinal/2^16)), and counting distinct segments — the document's own note states a qualitative guarantee (N ≥ 2^16 implies different segments) but not this specific count.

questions.question: A directory's top-level record sequence contains a record whose type field is 0x1234 (inside the reserved range 0x0003-0x7FFF) with MUST_UNDERSTAND = 0. Must a conforming reader reject the file because of this record? Separately, is the file nonetheless nonconforming, and if so, under which §21.2 row, what outcome class, and whose detector (reader or verifier)?
questions.answer_form: a yes/no plus a row label, outcome-class name, and detector name
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the subtle point that a verifier-detected row's stated outcome class names where the damage is recorded, not a reader obligation — a reader with MU=0 ignores the record exactly as for any unassigned type, yet the file is still nonconforming at file scope.

questions.question: A layer stored at least one tile in the generation a commit supersedes. The commit attempts to shrink one of that layer's dimension extents (and change nothing else). Name the only two ways this specific change may legitimately be accomplished, per §20.3 step 4.
questions.answer_form: an ordered or unordered list of exactly two named outcomes
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the closed-list exception that a stored-tile layer's declarations are mostly frozen, with extent growth (never shrink) one of the few exceptions, so shrinking can only happen via a new layer or a whole-file rewrite.

questions.question: An updater implements an unregistered record type (0x1234, outside §7.3's registry) according to that type's own external definition, which fixes MU = 0, PE = 1 for it. In the file, this record's stored flags happen to read MU = 0, PE = 0, and the updater's commit does not logically modify the record. Which flags govern — the stored bits, or the type's own definition — and may the updater drop the record from its output?
questions.answer_form: a verdict naming which flags govern plus a yes/no on dropping
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the three-way authority rule for which flags govern a record (registry-fixed, for a type the updater implements from its own definition, or stored-bits-as-authoritative for a type the updater does not implement) applied to the middle case, which is easy to collapse into the other two.

questions.question: Per R-VEC-04, every conformance vector whose recorded outcome is reject-layer must be built inside a file that also carries what additional element, and what must the manifest record about that element?
questions.answer_form: a short phrase naming the element plus what must be recorded about it
questions.why_it_matters: Tests a structural requirement on the conformance corpus itself — a reject-layer vector is meaningless without an intact sibling whose decoded content is also recorded, since otherwise a whole-file rejection would pass the same vector.

questions.question: During one region-read request against an interleaved layer, a reader has already returned decoded values for several tiles earlier in that same request, then reaches a tile whose segment CRC fails verification. questions.question: A file's total size is 2,000,000 bytes. Its trailer gives dir_offset = 1,998,900 and dir_length = 120. questions.question: A writer emits a top-level record with type value 0x8123. (a) Classify this value as assigned, reserved, or experimental. (b) If a reader does not implement this type and the record's stored MUST_UNDERSTAND bit is 1, what must the reader do, and does the file count as nonconforming on account of this record? questions.why_it_matters: Tests the carve-out between the reserved range (whose emission is always a violation) and the experimental range (whose emission is writer-conduct, never a bytes violation, even at MU=1 where the reader still must reject) — a rule stated only in prose split across two sections and a non-violations table.

questions.question: A layer declares rank 2 with dimensions, in declared order, y (extent 300, tile extent 64) and x (extent 500, tile extent 128); channel count C = 5; layout = planar; index_encoding = 1. Compute, in order: the grid counts G_y and G_x; the spatial-tile count N; the addressed-tile count (entry_count); and the tile-index region's extent_length in bytes. Give all five as integers.

questions.question: Using the same layer as the previous question (G_y = 5, G_x = 4, N = 20, C = 5, planar, dimensions declared in order (y, x)), find the disk ordinal of the tile that carries channel index 3 at tile coordinates (t_y = 2, t_x = 1). Show the spatial ordinal s and the final disk ordinal as two integers.
questions.answer_form: Two integers: s, then the disk ordinal.
questions.why_it_matters: Applies the row-major spatial-ordinal formula (which dimension varies fastest is fixed by declared order, not by axis label) and the planar channel-major disk-ordinal formula together, on a fresh case.

questions.question: A layer declares codec 4 (lz4), rank 1, one dimension with extent 0 and tile extent 2,200,000,000, one channel of type uint8. (a) Is this declaration, as stated, conforming? Name the rule that decides it. (b) If a later commit grows that dimension's extent from 0 to 1 (nothing else about the layer changes), is the resulting generation's declaration for this layer still conforming? Give a yes/no for (a) and (b), each with the one governing requirement identifier or section.

questions.question: A layer is planar with channel count C = 4 and spatial-tile count N = 20,000 (so entry_count = 80,000). Using the channel-major disk-ordinal rule and a segment size of 2^16 entries, find: the disk ordinal of the tile-index entry addressing channel index 3 at spatial ordinal 19,999; which segment index (0-based) contains that entry; and that segment's entry range as a half-open interval of entry indices.

questions.question: A planar bool channel has P = 20 sample positions per tile and a declared fill value of true (0x01). The four real (non-padding) values at in-tile ordinals 16, 17, 18, 19 are, respectively, false, true, false, false. Give the exact value, as a single hex byte (upper-case hex digits, e.g. 0xAB), of the tile's third decoded byte (byte index 2, zero-based), including its pad bits.
questions.answer_form: One hex byte, upper-case digits, in 0xNN form.
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the LSB-first bit-packing rule for a planar bool plane with the fixed-to-fill content rule for pad bits, on specific non-padding values the document's own example does not use.

questions.question: For a planar bool channel (a packed boolean plane), what shuffle stride does the byte-shuffle filter use, and — independent of whether the layer's declared filter value is "none" or "byte-shuffle" — is the filtered image for such a plane ever different from its unfiltered decoded image? Answer with the stride value and a yes/no.
questions.answer_form: An integer stride value, then yes/no.
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the carve-out that packed boolean planes always take stride 1, making the byte-shuffle filter the identity regardless of which filter value a layer declares — a quantifier easy to lose in a rewording.

questions.question: Two layer records in one directory have name fields whose raw bytes are both the 3-byte sequence 61 00 62 (which contains the C0 control byte 0x00, itself independently invalid as a name). At open, does the reader treat these two layer records as a duplicate-name violation? If so, state the outcome class, and state whether the name field's own invalidity changes or defers that determination.
questions.answer_form: A yes/no, an outcome-class name, and one sentence on whether invalidity defers the duplicate check.
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the explicit prose rule that layer-name uniqueness is decided first and over raw bytes whether or not either name is itself well-formed — a rule a careless summary could invert by assuming invalid names are excluded from the uniqueness comparison.

questions.question: A layer currently stores at least one tile, under codec = zstd (3), tile extents (128, 128). A single appender commit attempts, at once: (a) growing one dimension's extent from 1000 to 1200, and (b) changing the layer's codec from zstd (3) to lz4 (4). Taking each change on its own merits as an appender operation (not a rewrite): is change (a) alone permitted? Is change (b) alone permitted? What must a writer that wants change (b) do instead?
questions.answer_form: Two yes/no verdicts for (a) and (b), then one short phrase naming the required alternative operation.
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the fixed-declarations list (which explicitly includes the codec) against the separately-stated permitted-changes list (which includes extent growth), applied to a single commit that mixes one of each.

questions.question: A rewriter is compacting a file and relocating one layer's stored tiles, which requires regenerating that layer's whole tile-index region. One index entry in that region is offset = sentinel, length not sentinel, crc = 0 — a malformed entry that the specification classifies reject-tile on a structural ground. Name the two, and only two, dispositions available to the rewriter for this situation, and say whether "carry this one entry forward unchanged while regenerating the rest of the region" is a third option.
questions.answer_form: An ordered list of exactly the two named dispositions, then a yes/no on the third-option question.
questions.why_it_matters: Tests whether the reader understands that a structurally malformed entry gives a rewriter nothing to re-point to, so per-entry repair or pass-through is foreclosed and only whole-layer drop or outright refusal remain.

questions.question: Summing the stated condition counts given at the head of each of §21.2 ("35 conditions"), §21.3 ("49 conditions"), §21.4 ("26 conditions"), and §21.5 ("10 conditions"), what total do you get, and does it match the total the specification states for the whole register in §21.8? Give the sum and a yes/no.
questions.answer_form: An integer sum, then yes/no.
questions.why_it_matters: A self-consistency check across five separate locations in the document; a rewording that silently changes any one subtotal, or the §21.8 total, breaks this arithmetic identity in a way a reader who checks only one location would miss.

questions.question: An appender is re-emitting the directory and meets a top-level record of type 0x0002 (user metadata) whose stored flag bits are MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1, PRESERVE_ON_EDIT = 0 — not the value the registry fixes for this type. For the purpose of deciding this record's persistence treatment in the commit (not its reader semantics), do the stored bits or the registry's fixed values govern? Name the applicable persistence-table row (by its MU/PE values) and what the appender must therefore do with the record's bytes.
questions.answer_form: A short verdict ("stored bits" or "registry values"), the row's MU/PE values, and one phrase for the required action.

findings.title: No stated priority among §6.2's grouped post-gate trailer checks
findings.detail: §6.2 states a strict sequence for exactly three gates (trailer magic, trailer CRC, version gate) and then introduces a distinct, larger set of checks — the flag gates, committed_file_length equality and multiple-of-64, dir_offset >= 16, dir_length >= 4, the offset+length bound, file_id != 0, reserved bytes all zero — under the heading 'the reader MUST validate all of the following,' with no ordering language among that group's own members. Every member independently yields reject-file, so the outcome class for a file failing several of them at once is unaffected, but which specific diagnostic (e.g. 'bad file_id' vs 'reserved bytes nonzero') a reader is to surface first when two or more of that group's conditions fail on the same file is not fixed by the text. I found this while testing, then discarding, a quiz question that would have asked 'which check is reported first' for a file failing two of these simultaneously; I could not derive a single determinate answer and dropped the question rather than force one.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST validate, in order: the trailer magic; the trailer CRC; the version gate (§6.3)... If those gates pass, the reader MUST validate all of the following before acting on the fields involved: the flag gates (§6.3); committed_file_length equals the file size...; dir_offset ≥ 16; dir_length ≥ 4; dir_offset + dir_length ≤ F − 64...; file_id ≠ 0; reserved bytes all zero. Any failure is reject-file.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is an internal-consistency observation about a single edition (B), not a two-edition comparison, so there is no byte or verdict in a second text to compare against; no quotation_b or location_b applies. It concerns diagnostic-reporting order among several reader checks that all share one outcome class, not a disputed byte value.

answers.reasoning: Worst-case pre-trailer pad before the next 64-byte boundary is 63 bytes, so dir_length ≤ 65,536 − 64 − 63 = 65,409.

answers.answer: F1, F6, F8, F14; total instances = 5
answers.decisive_quote: Deriving it there yields F8, F14, F6 and both of F1's instances — each asserting an invariant `[R-CNT-24]` fixes in every major — and no other row.
answers.reasoning: F1 has two instances (front signature block, trailer magic), F6, F8, F14 one instance each: 2+1+1+1=5.

answers.decisive_quote: A commit's committed_file_length is strictly greater than the prior trailer's, by at least 128
answers.reasoning: 1,048,576 + 128 = 1,048,704 = 0x100080, the minimum legal next value.

answers.decisive_quote: the disk tile ordinal ... is s for an interleaved layer, and c · N + s for a planar layer ... where c is the channel's index — channel-major grouping
interleaved | P · Q | (k div C) · Q + F_{k mod C}
Every pad bit (§14.3) MUST carry the plane's channel's fill bit.
answers.reasoning: 20 real values all false fill bytes 0 and 1 and low nibble of byte 2 with zeros; fill=true sets the 4 pad bits (bits 4-7 of byte 2) to 1, giving 0xF0.

answers.answer: Nonconforming; reject-layer; layer; yes
answers.decisive_quote: Writers MUST NOT declare this codec for a layer any of whose addressed tiles' decoded size exceeds 0x7E000000 bytes ... a reader MUST treat such a declaration as a validity error at layer scope, checkable from declarations alone.

findings.detail: A reader that does not implement a core, assigned codec (e.g. zstd, codec 3) is declared outright not to be a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03]), full stop - this is correct and unambiguous. But the document never says what such software (which still exists and must do something) is permitted to do: may it still serve requests against the file's other layers, or list this layer's declarations without decoding it? For the structurally parallel case of a conforming VERIFIER that cannot execute a codec, the document gives a complete protocol (section 17.4: cannot certify, report 'cannot establish', narrow the claim) - it extends no equivalent courtesy, or even a cross-reference, to an ordinary reader in the same position. Two independently-built, otherwise-conformant-except-for-this-codec readers given the identical file could reasonably diverge: one rejects the whole file (having no stated authority to scope its own disqualification), the other serves every other layer and lists this one's declarations (reasoning by analogy from [R-ERR-04]'s narrowest-scope resource-decline pattern and from section 17.4's verifier treatment). The document decides between neither.

But section 10.1's closed, four-item list of the only ways this format grows names, as its sole trailer-flag vehicle, 'New ignore-lane flag bits' - never incompat-lane bits - and [R-EXT-01] closes the list ('Nothing else extends this format'). Every mention of the incompat lane in the document (seven places) describes it only as currently all-zero with any set bit always rejected (F19), never as something a minor-version vehicle can ever populate; and since [R-CNT-24] lets a future MAJOR version redefine the whole 48-byte trailer remainder anyway (flags field included), a future major does not need these specific 16 bits pre-reserved either. probe_answers.answer: The scenario's premise cannot occur for a conforming reader: codecs 1–4, zstd (3) included, are all core and a conforming reader MUST implement every one of them. Software unable to execute an assigned codec "is not a conforming reader" at all — there is no register row or outcome class assigned to this case because it falls outside the conformance classes entirely, rather than being an in-scope outcome with an answer. The adjacent, in-register case — codec field value from the reserved (5–0x7FFF) or experimental (≥0x8000) range — is a plain validity error at layer scope (register row L43), reject-layer: other layers remain fully servable and the reader MAY still list the rejected layer's name, but that is not this scenario, since codec 3 is an assigned, core value.

findings.title: Exact byte offsets of appended regions within one commit are writer-chosen, not fixed
findings.detail: The append procedure fixes the ordered sequence of high-level steps (payloads+indexes, then directory, then pad+trailer) and the overall step order, but the relative placement/offsets of a layer's new payload versus its new index region, and the interleaving of multiple changed layers' structures within one commit, are left to R-SLB-05's placement freedom whenever no alignment/slab is declared. An implementer building Probe W2's byte-offset table from the document alone cannot derive a single fixed set of offsets (only fixed sizes and a fixed high-level ordering) — two conforming appenders doing the identical logical edit will legitimately diverge in exact offsets, which is intentional per R-CNF-05/R-SLB-05 but worth flagging since it bounds how precise a 'byte layout' answer to W2 can be.
findings.quotation_a: Writers MUST NOT emit any other value ... That freedom is over *ordering and relative position*, and a byte the live state does not claim is slack whatever produced it (§5.2).
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It changes which exact bytes (offsets) a conforming appender may emit for the identical logical edit — two implementations will legitimately diverge in offsets though never in validity, which bears directly on how two implementers' byte-level walks of W2 could differ without either being wrong.

findings.title: Creator-vs-rewriter status is a self-declared position, not a function of what bytes a tool actually reproduces
findings.detail: A tool that reads an existing file and writes a new one can choose to be a 'creator' (flags=0, no preservation duty, answers for every byte including ones copied from the input) or a 'rewriter' (must preserve per §20.4/§20.5, carries forward unknown ignore-lane bits), and the document states this is the tool's own choice rather than something determined by how much of the input content it reproduces. Two implementers building semantically similar 'read-and-regenerate' tools could legitimately produce different flags-handling behavior purely by labelling their own code path differently, with no byte-level test in the document to adjudicate which label a given tool actually is.

findings.title: A barred fill-value change on a stored-tile layer is undetectable when the layer has no padding tiles
findings.detail: §20.3 bars a commit from changing a stored-tile layer's channel fill, but states explicitly that this writer-conduct bar does not by itself make a file nonconforming; the only detection mechanism the document names is T4 (`[R-SER-05]`), which checks that a padding position's bytes still encode the channel's current fill. Padding positions exist only in edge tiles where a dimension's extent does not divide its tile extent exactly (§11.3). For a layer whose every dimension's extent divides its tile extent exactly — a layer with no edge tiles at all — no padding position exists for any channel, so T4 (and every other register row) has nothing to check, and a conforming reader or verifier accepts the resulting file without exception. An implementation can therefore violate the fill-change bar and still produce a file every check in §21 certifies, with no trace distinguishing it from a file that never changed. A layer with dimension/tile-extent pairs that divide evenly (e.g. extent 256, tile extent 256: grid count 1, no overhang) stores a tile, then an appender's commit changes only that channel's declared fill value, leaving the stored tile's bytes untouched. The resulting file passes the trailer, directory, index-chain, and every T1-T26 register check; a conforming verifier certifies it. Two implementations given the same 'do not change fill' instruction thus diverge at the byte level — one emits the forbidden change, one does not — and nothing in the file distinguishes them nor does any check reject the one that violated the rule.
findings.quotation_a: "A commit MUST NOT change one of these; the change is a new layer, or a rewrite that re-declares it under a fresh file_id ... This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself."

findings.byte_level_rationale: This decides whether a conforming reader must accept a given byte sequence (post-fill-change, no-padding case) as fully valid — it must, by the document's own register, even though the writer action that produced it is explicitly forbidden conduct; an implementer relying on T4 to catch every fill-change violation would wrongly assume this case is also caught.

findings.title: Whether MU=1/PE=0 fixed by an implemented-but-unregistered type's own definition still forces no-drop retention is stated two ways
findings.detail: §7.2's Note states, apparently unconditionally, that `[R-CNT-12]` collapses every record into three states because 'MU = 1, whose PE bit is read as 1 whatever is stored' — tying that collapse directly to §20.4's three table rows with no carve-out. §20.4 itself, discussing a type the updater implements but this specification does not register, says the opposite for that case: 'the definition it implements the type from supplies the flags, and the stored bits never do ... so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites' — explicitly removing implemented types from the no-drop MU=1 row and letting PE=0 alone license a drop. For a record whose governing definition fixes MU=1 and PE=0, the two passages select different outcomes: the Note's logic would retain the record byte-identically with no drop permitted, while §20.4's explicit carve-out would let the updater drop it. An updater implements an unregistered record type X from a third-party specification that assigns X the flags MU=1, PE=0; in a commit that does not otherwise touch the scope X governs, it wants to drop a stale X record. One implementer reads 'so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites' and drops it (PE=0 licenses a drop); another reads the §7.2 Note's unconditional MU=1-collapses-PE-to-1 rule and retains it byte-identically, refusing to drop. Both implementers can point to an exact sentence for their behavior, and the two resulting files (one with the record present, one without) cannot both be the unique conforming output of the same commit, so at most one reading is the specification's intent, and the document does not say which.
findings.quotation_a: "[R-CNT-12] leaves a record three states, not four, and they are §20.4's three rows: MU = 1, whose PE bit is read as 1 whatever is stored" versus "Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement ... so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: This decides whether a conforming updater's commit that drops such a record (or, symmetrically, retains it) is the one the specification licenses — i.e., whether the record's bytes may legally be absent from, or must be present in, the next commit's directory. The two readings produce different, mutually exclusive sets of bytes a conforming updater may emit for the same input.

probe_answers.answer: Exactly three verdicts, per the Conforming-verifier definition in Sec.2.3: (1) conforming -- produced when the verifier has established no violation anywhere and has nothing left unchecked on a capability/resource ground (e.g. the minimal 128-byte file with zero layers, valid trailer and directory CRCs, satisfies every requirement and the walk completes with nothing uncheckable); (2) nonconforming -- produced whenever the verifier has established at least one violation, 'however many requirements it was unable to check' (e.g. a stored tile's bytes failing its index entry's CRC, condition T1, R-CNT-20); (3) cannot establish -- produced when some requirement is one the verifier is unable to check on a capability or resource ground AND no violation was established elsewhere (e.g. a verifier that cannot execute a layer's declared codec, R-COD-11, Sec.17.4). A fourth label, 'unexamined', names scopes not looked at after an early stop but 'is neither a verdict nor cannot establish -- it constrains the report, not the verdict' (Sec.2.3).
probe_answers.citations: Sec.2.3 (Conforming verifier definition, R-CNF-11); Sec.21.4 row T1 (R-CNT-20); Sec.17.4 (R-COD-11)
probe_answers.decisive_quote: A verifier reports one of three verdicts: *conforming*, *nonconforming*, or *cannot establish* ... An established violation takes priority: a verifier that has established any violation reports *nonconforming*, however many requirements it was unable to check, and *cannot establish* is available only to a traversal that established no violation.

probe_answers.answer: Reserved range (0x0003-0x7FFF) + MU=1: the file is itself nonconforming (not merely rejected on capability grounds) -- emitting any reserved-range value is a violation whatever its MU bit (row F36, verifier-detected), and the MU=1 combination specifically is also, and more narrowly, row F35 (reader-detected, at open); by Sec.21.1's own 'strict specialization' rule ('F35 of F36' is named explicitly as such a pair) the file is recorded against the narrower F35 alone. A reader rejects the file at open under R-CNT-15's unknown-type/MU=1 gate, and this rejection is itself evidence of nonconformance, not a bare capability refusal. The fix: Sec.10.3, 'a value from a reserved range MUST NOT be emitted at all before this specification assigns it'; also Sec.2.3, 'in a conforming file such a type is necessarily from the experimental range, since a reserved-range type carrying MU = 1 is itself a violation.' -- Experimental range (>=0x8000) + MU=1: the reader still rejects the file (reject-file, under the same R-CNT-15 MU=1 gate) but the file remains fully conforming -- this is explicitly the second of Sec.21.6's 'two structural cases: conforming files a reader nevertheless refuses.' For a verifier, this is one of the named 'cannot establish' grounds in Sec.2.3 ('when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (Sec.21.6)'), provided no other violation is established. There is no 'fix' required of the writer here -- nothing is wrong with the file; Sec.10.3 only cautions that experimental values carry no collision protection and are private-use, so a writer wanting the type broadly understood would register it (Sec.10.4) rather than rely on the experimental range, but this is not a conformance requirement.
probe_answers.citations: Sec.21.1 (specialization clause, 'F35 of F36'); Sec.21.2 rows F35, F36 (R-CNT-15); Sec.7.2 (R-CNT-15 unknown-type MU gate); Sec.2.3 (reserved-range-under-MU=1 sentence; cannot-establish grounds); Sec.10.3 (R-EXT-03, no-emission rule); Sec.21.6 ('two structural cases')
probe_answers.decisive_quote: The qualifier is load-bearing -- the same type as a layer sub-record is reject-layer and never a ground to refuse the file ... since the prohibition on publishing experimental values binds a writer's conduct and not the bytes.

probe_answers.answer: Assumptions: neither layer declares per-tile alignment (A=0) nor a slab (S=0) -- nothing in the probe states otherwise and R-SLB-05 leaves placement unconstrained absent such a declaration -- so tiles, index region and directory are each written back-to-back with no internal gap; the only gap per commit is the pre-trailer pad rounding the directory's end up to the next 64-byte boundary (R-LIF-02 step 5), content unconstrained/zeroed-by-advisory (R-CNT-03) either way. Index-region-size formula (entry_count*20+ceil(entry_count/65536)*4) backs out entry_count=4 for A (84B) and entry_count=8 for B (164B). Tracing the three commits (first begins at offset 16; each later one begins at the prior F; a commit that supersedes a stored tile re-emits that layer's whole index region at a new placement, R-WRT-04; an untouched layer's record and region carry forward unmoved, R-WRT-05): gen 1 -> F1=4,480 (pad 20B); gen 2 (adds B, A untouched) -> F2=13,120 (pad 20B); gen 3 (supersedes one 1,024B tile of A, A's whole index re-emitted, B untouched) -> F3=14,528 (pad 36B). Live-state byte total = 12,816 (front 16 + A's live tiles 4,096 + A's live index 84 + B's live tiles 8,192 + B's live index 164 + live directory 200 + live trailer 64). Slack total = 1,712 (gen-1's directory+pad+trailer 284 + gen-2's directory+pad+trailer 284 + gen-3's pad 36 + the superseded 1,024B A tile + A's superseded gen-1 index region 84). Check: 12,816+1,712=14,528=F3.
probe_answers.citations: Sec.7.4 (index-region-size formula, R-CNT-17); Sec.9.2 (commit protocol order, R-LIF-02); Sec.20.3 (R-WRT-04, R-WRT-05); Sec.16 (R-SLB-05, placement otherwise unconstrained); Sec.5.2/Sec.9.7 (live state vs slack, R-CNT-21)
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Writers MUST place the directory so that no structure lies between its end and the trailer. Those bytes -- the pre-trailer pad -- are slack ... bounds their number only through step 5 of the commit protocol, which pads to the next 64-byte boundary.

probe_answers.answer: If the verifier has established no other violation anywhere in the file, the verdict on the whole file is cannot establish -- not nonconforming and not conforming -- specifically because the decoded-content obligations of Sec.14 (R-SER-05, R-SER-08) require decoding, and a verifier that cannot execute that layer's codec (or filter) cannot establish that layer's conformance and must not certify. If some other violation was already established elsewhere, the overall verdict is nonconforming regardless (the priority rule of Sec.2.3), and the codec limitation is reported alongside it. Either way, the report names, for that layer, the requirement it could not check and the ground: the codec (or filter) value it could not execute, per Sec.2.3's unconditional per-requirement reporting duty. This scenario is realistic only for a reserved- or experimental-range codec/filter value: for every assigned (core) codec and filter, software unable to execute it 'is not a conforming reader' at all (R-CNF-03), so an actual conforming verifier's inability to execute is confined to values outside the core, assigned set.
probe_answers.citations: Sec.17.4 (R-COD-11); Sec.2.3 (cannot-establish definition and per-requirement reporting duty, priority rule); Sec.2.3 (R-CNF-03, core codec/filter obligation)
probe_answers.decisive_quote: A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file. That inability is not a finding that the file is nonconforming, and it fixes the file's verdict as *cannot establish* only where the verifier established no violation elsewhere.

probe_answers.answer: No -- a verifier cannot see that 'the last commit' did anything in particular, because it never enumerates prior commits at all: it walks only the live trailer and what it reaches from it, and the document is explicit that this does not depend on reconstructing the file's history. Beyond that, the specific conduct this probe describes (a commit changing a fixed declaration -- a fill value, a type, a tile extent, etc. -- of a layer that stored a tile) is a bar on the appender as an actor, not a register row: 'no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself ... the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit.' Its effects on the resulting live state are, by the document's own account, almost entirely unwitnessed: every checksum in Sec.8 certifies whatever bytes were actually written, and the only ways any trace of the change can surface are a named, closed list of other register rows that happen to also be tripped -- a changed decoded size, a changed window/content-size declaration, broken padding/pad-bit/boolean-byte content, or a codec/filter framing check under a changed codec/filter (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2, T17, T24, T25). Absent one of those incidental trips, the resulting file can certify as conforming on its own terms even though the writer violated this conduct rule -- the verifier simply has no instrument pointed at the condition itself.
probe_answers.citations: Sec.9.7 note (history not reconstructed); Sec.20.3 ('The line is drawn...' paragraph and the 'This bar binds the commit as an actor' paragraph); Sec.20.4 Rationale (adjacency of generations not recoverable); Sec.21.7 ('what no check detects')
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Nothing here enumerates prior commits. A verifier certifies what a reader can reach and counts what it cannot, which is decidable from the live trailer in one pass and does not depend on reconstructing the file's history.

probe_answers.answer: The combination (MU=1 with PE=0) is itself a writer violation that makes the file nonconforming, but it changes no reader-facing behavior at all: per R-CNT-12, 'a reader or updater encountering it MUST treat the record as PE = 1 (never silently deletable)' -- the record is simply never silently dropped, by any actor, regardless of what bits are stored. Because conforming behavior is unchanged, detecting the combination is assigned to the verifier alone, which 'MUST treat ... the MU = 1 with PE = 0 combination as a validity error at the record's governing scope.' The scope depends on which record carries the combination: file scope if it is a non-layer top-level record (register row F25, outcome reject-file-as-recorded-by-the-verifier) or layer scope if it is a layer record or one of that layer's sub-records (register row L46, outcome reject-layer-as-recorded). In either case this is a verifier-only-detected row, so per Sec.21.1 'the outcome names the scope at which the damage is recorded, not an obligation on any reader' -- no reader is required to refuse anything, though R-CNF-12's licence to reject any detected violation on a nonconforming file remains available to one that notices it anyway.
probe_answers.citations: Sec.7.2 (R-CNT-12, the MU=1/PE=0 reading rule); Sec.21.1 (verifier-only-row clarification); Sec.21.2 row F25; Sec.21.3 row L46
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Writers MUST NOT emit the combination MU = 1 with PE = 0; a reader or updater encountering it MUST treat the record as PE = 1 (never silently deletable) ... their detection is a verifier's: a verifier MUST treat a nonzero reserved flag bit or the MU = 1 with PE = 0 combination as a validity error at the record's governing scope.

findings.title: Sec.2.4 labels every register outcome a 'reader outcome' without qualification; Sec.21.1 narrows this for verifier-only rows
findings.detail: Sec.2.4 states unqualified: every detectable violation 'is assigned exactly one reader outcome: reject-file, reject-layer, reject-tile, or ignore-record.' Over 3,000 lines later, Sec.21.1 narrows this for the ~20 rows whose Detector is verifier: 'the outcome names the scope at which the damage is recorded, not an obligation on any reader' -- for such rows a reader that serves the data unchanged is still conforming (Sec.21.1 names R-CNT-22 and R-MTA-05 as rows the reader 'serves ... unchanged'). An implementation built from Sec.2.4's definition and the register's bare Outcome column, without separately applying Sec.21.1's Detector-keyed carve-out, would wrongly refuse scopes (e.g. a layer whose only defect is L49, a stored-flags/registry mismatch) that this specification requires a conforming reader to serve.
findings.quotation_a: Every detectable file-conformance violation named by this specification is assigned exactly one **reader outcome**: reject-file, reject-layer, reject-tile, or ignore-record.
findings.quotation_b: For a row whose Detector is *verifier*, the outcome names the scope at which the damage is recorded, not an obligation on any reader.
findings.byte_level_rationale: A reader that treats every Outcome-column entry (including verifier-only rows like L49, F28, L46-L49, T2/T4/T5/T26) as its own refusal obligation would reject and fail to serve scopes this document requires a conforming reader to serve unchanged; a reader that correctly applies Sec.21.1's carve-out would serve them. That is a real difference in which bytes a conforming implementation returns for the same input file, turning on which of the two passages (read in isolation vs. together) governs the implementer's behavior.

findings.location_a: Sec.20.3 ('The line is drawn where a stored tile's meaning is fixed' paragraph)
findings.location_b: Sec.9.7 (note on not enumerating prior commits)
findings.title: A changed fixed declaration over a stored tile is, by the document's own consistent account, almost entirely unwitnessed
findings.detail: Probe V5 turns on this: the document states, in two separate sections that agree with each other, that (a) a verifier's walk never sees commit history at all, only the live state reached from the live trailer, so whether 'the last commit' changed anything is not a question any check asks; and (b) even within the one generation a verifier does see, the consequences of such a change are invisible except where they incidentally trip one of a named, closed set of other register rows (decoded-size/window/content-size/padding/pad-bit/boolean-byte/codec-framing rows T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2, T17, T24, T25). This is not a contradiction -- it is the document's own, repeated, and consistent description of its own detection boundary -- but it is the decisive, load-bearing fact behind answering V5, and worth recording plainly: a verifier implementation that tried to detect 'did an update change fixed declarations' as its own check would be building something this specification affirmatively does not provide.
findings.quotation_a: Under new [declarations] the same bytes would denote values, coordinates or padding the writer did not store, with every checksum in Sec.8 certifying the result and ... no check any actor owes able to see it (Sec.21.7).
findings.quotation_b: Nothing here enumerates prior commits. A verifier certifies what a reader can reach and counts what it cannot, which is decidable from the live trailer in one pass and does not depend on reconstructing the file's history.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Resolving this does not change what bytes a conforming implementation may emit, accept, or reject: the specification already fixes the answer unambiguously (no check sees the condition directly; only its incidental fallout through the named rules is caught), and two readers who each read the whole document would reach the identical implementation. I report it as an observation describing the decisive mechanism behind a probe answer, not as an unresolved question.

(b) One of the four assigned core values (1-4) that this particular verifier's implementation genuinely cannot execute: section17.4 fixes verdict cannot establish (assuming no violation found elsewhere), report naming the codec and the capability ground; but R-CNF-03 ('software that declines any of those is not a conforming reader') means a tool in this branch, for an assigned value, is never actually a conforming verifier in the document's own terms -- the branch exists for non-conforming software's reporting discipline, not as a status a conforming verifier can occupy for values 1-4.

probe_answers.answer: No, not directly: the verifier's coverage walk (section9.7) never reconstructs history or compares generations, and the bar itself is stated to leave no file-conformance condition at all ('no register row records the violation itself...the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit'). What verdict follows depends on symptom: where the re-declaration also breaks an ordinary, already-registered content check (decoded size, padding fill, pad bits, boolean-byte validity, or a codec/filter framing check: T2/T3/T4/T5/T14/T17/T21/T22/T24/T25), the verifier does find a violation and reports nonconforming via that row -- with no indication in the report that the cause was an illegal re-declaration. Where it produces no such symptom (the document's own example: a bare name change, or two channel names swapped), the condition is genuinely unwitnessed and the verifier reports conforming (or cannot-establish only on an unrelated ground).

probe_answers.answer: The verifier treats MU=1/PE=0 as an established validity error at the record's governing scope: file scope for a non-layer top-level record (register row F25, verifier/certification) or layer scope for a layer record or layer sub-record (register row L46, verifier/certification), both under R-CNT-12. Ordinary reader behavior is unaffected -- the record is still read as PE=1, never silently deletable -- but the file becomes nonconforming (R-CNF-05) once this combination is found, and R-CNT-12 already requires every reader/updater, not only verifiers, to treat such a record as PE=1 regardless of what is stored.
probe_answers.citations: section 7.2 (the MU=1/PE=0 paragraph); section 21.2 row F25; section 21.3 row L46; section 21.1's closing remarks; R-CNT-12, R-CNF-05
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Both writer violations make the file nonconforming (R-CNF-05) while leaving conforming behavior unchanged, so their detection is a verifier's: a verifier MUST treat a nonzero reserved flag bit or the MU = 1 with PE = 0 combination as a validity error at the record's governing scope.

Both editions are, for every passage either reader-walk cites across all eight probes (R1-R8), byte-for-byte identical in substance: reflowed to different line widths, with clauses occasionally reordered within a sentence, but never differing in what is decided. I opened every cited passage directly in both files and confirmed §6.2-6.4/§7.1/§19.1 (R1), §6.2-6.3 and register row F19 (R2), §15.1-15.3 and row T7 (R4), §7.1/§2.4 and row F20 (R5), §5.1 and row F5 (R6), §11.2/§11.4/§14.2 (R7), and §2.3-2.4/§21.6 and rows F35/F36/L24/L25 (R8) are all EQUIVALENT between editions.

The one place the two walks' answers genuinely diverge (R3, a conforming reader unable to execute a core, assigned codec) is not a textual difference. §17.4's governing sentence — "For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer (R-COD-03, R-COD-09); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (R-CNF-03)" — is present word for word in both editions, at the exact line range (2634-2646 in A) walker A itself cites as containing "no equivalent text... to an ordinary reader." Walker A's transcript quotes only the preceding verifier-focused half of §17.4 and then asserts the reader case is undecided (its Finding readera-01, marked AMBIGUITY); walker B, reading the byte-identical sentence in edition B, found and correctly used it to answer R3 as resolved. This is REPORTER_ERROR by walker A, not an edition difference — both texts decide R3 identically.

A second, genuine (if byte-level-inert) difference: edition A's §2.3 carries a worked Note, immediately after R-CNF-13's "reach" definition, deriving example-by-example why F14 reaches other format majors while F5 and F15 (despite citing R-CNT-24) do not. This Note is entirely absent from edition B (confirmed by direct search; zero hits). Both editions' §21.2 opening states the conclusion identically ("Deriving it there yields F8, F14, F6 and both of F1's instances... and no other row"), so no register row's outcome differs and no implementation built from either edition diverges in behavior. But walker B's own transcript shows it independently re-deriving exactly this reasoning under R6 ("I checked this because I expected F5 might be a fifth 'reaches-every-major' row... it does not name F5 among the four") — a guess edition A does not force on its reader, since A simply states the worked derivation. I also checked readera-02 (the incompat-lane-unpopulatable OBSERVATION) against edition B and found the supporting text identically present in both; walker B simply did not report it, which is a walk-thoroughness gap, not a fidelity defect. A further, lower-confidence note: edition A's §2.3 "Conforming TARN file" bullet names four specific writer-conduct-only cases that B's corresponding bullet states only generally; I spot-checked one (the ignore-lane-flags conduct rule) and found it preserved verbatim at its own section in both editions, supporting reorganization over loss, but I did not individually re-verify all four, so I report it with lower confidence than the other findings.

findings.title: Edition B drops A's worked derivation of which register rows 'reach' other format majors
findings.detail: Edition A follows R-CNF-13's abstract 'reach' test with a Note working it by hand over three named rows: F14 reaches (it checksums bytes a future major may redefine, but asserts only R-CNT-24's fixed CRC invariant); F5 does not reach (its 128-byte floor is derived from format-major-1-specific structure sizes, even though its subject, physical file size, is not itself redefinable); F15 does not reach despite its Governing-rule cell citing R-CNT-24 (the specific reserved bytes it checks are inside the part of the trailer R-CNT-24 lets a future major redefine). Edition B has no corresponding Note anywhere in or after §2.3 (confirmed by search: zero hits for this reasoning's key phrases in B's §2.3 region). Both editions' §21.2 opening paragraph states the bottom-line conclusion identically ('Deriving it there yields F8, F14, F6 and both of F1's instances... and no other row'), so no register row's assigned outcome differs between editions — but an implementer of B who wants to understand (or extend) why the test sorts rows this way, rather than take the conclusion on faith, must re-derive A's three-example reasoning from scratch. Walker B's own transcript shows exactly this forced re-derivation happening under R6: 'I checked this because I expected F5 might be a fifth reaches-every-major row... it does not name F5 among the four... I [worked out] this is because R-CNT-27's check needs no byte of the file's content' — independently reconstructing, unprompted, what A's Note simply states.
findings.quotation_a: The test is the invariant a condition violates, not the fields it reads, and three rows show why the distinction carries the weight. §21.2's F14 reaches although the bytes it checksums include fields a future major may redefine: it consumes them as CRC input and asserts only [R-CNT-24]'s CRC-32C at F - 4 over [F - 64, F - 4). F5 does not reach although its subject is the physical file size, which no major can redefine: the 128-byte floor it asserts is derived from a directory of at least 4 bytes at an offset of at least 16 and a 64-aligned F ([R-CNT-27]), and those are format major 1's. F15 does not reach although its Governing rule cell cites [R-CNT-24]: the trailer bytes it requires be zero are inside the 48 that rule lets a future major redefine.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: B's §21.2 opening states the same conclusion (which specific rows reach) in the same words as A's, so every register row's assigned outcome, and hence every byte a conforming implementation accepts or rejects for the current rule set, is identical between editions. The loss is of the worked justification an implementer or future ADR author would need to correctly classify a *new* condition's reach without re-deriving the test from scratch — a loss of determinacy/explanatory support, not of a currently-decided byte-level outcome.

result.summary:
I read edition A (5004 lines) and edition B (4810 lines) in full and swept for completeness section by section. Method: (1) compared the full heading outline of both editions, which found B reorders §3 before §2 (a pure order change) and, more significantly, that A's entire §3.3 subsection has no counterpart anywhere in B; (2) censused every block labelled Note/Example/Rationale in both editions by fingerprint (A: 94, B: 90), pairing 89 one-to-one, finding one genuinely new block in B, and resolving the remaining five unpaired A blocks by direct reading — four are simply gone and one survives reworded outside its blockquote; the arithmetic (94 − 5 + 1 = 90) closes the census exactly; (3) wrote a de-wrapping script that joins each hard-wrapped paragraph (respecting blockquotes, tables, headings, lists, fences) into one line per paragraph, split both editions into per-subsection files by heading number, and ran `diff -u` on every matched pair — 97 of ~115 subsections produced a hunk, all read in file order, the other 18 confirmed byte-identical; (4) for every hunk that looked like it might narrow, widen, or drop a rule rather than just reword it, re-read both editions side-by-side and ran targeted control greps across both whole files to prove whether the content survived elsewhere; (5) ran a keyword-frequency control (MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY, REQUIRED, SHALL) over both whole documents as a cheap check against a silently flipped modal verb — MUST/MUST NOT/MAY/REQUIRED/SHALL matched exactly; SHOULD was off by one, traced to a single sentence in §6.3 where B spells out as its own sentence an obligation A had left as an elided zeugma ("a writer SHOULD emit X ... and an appender [SHOULD emit] Y"), not a new obligation.

The sweep found four genuine LOSSes, all non-normative (Note) material in edition A that is simply absent from edition B with no restatement found anywhere by targeted grep: (1) §2.3's trailing Note, which illustrated the "invariant, not bytes read" cross-major-reach test with three worked rows (F14 reaches, F5 and F15 do not) — B's §21.2 states the same final list of reaching rows verbatim in both editions, so no accept/reject verdict differs, but the worked derivation that would let an implementer generalize the test to a new row is gone; (2) §2.4's one-sentence Note clarifying that "reject" names a scope of unusability and not a mandated user-interface behavior — dropped with no replacement found anywhere in B; (3) A's entire §3.3 subsection ("Container and array model"), a Note stating that Part I is independent of Part II by construction and that this independence is "load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20" — the whole subsection, heading included, has vanished, and targeted greps for its key phrases turn up nothing in B; (4) §4.4's trailing Note disambiguating that the general bit-numbering rule (R-ENC-08) does not itself govern boolean sample-bit mapping (a separate §14 rule) — dropped, though lower severity since §14.3 already cites "(§4.4)" directly for its own bit order in both editions. A fifth, related LOSS: when A's §2.3 "Conforming verifier" bullet's cannot-establish grounds relocate to a new closing paragraph in B's §21.6, the move carries the five positive grounds over but drops the one negative carve-out (that an experimental-range user-metadata encoding is explicitly not such a ground) — recoverable from an unchanged table row elsewhere in §21.6, so no verdict differs, but the explicit sentence is gone.

I also logged, at lower priority, one genuine ADDITION (a new Rationale in §15.4 with two new worked MiB figures, both arithmetically derivable from facts A itself states) and one label change worth noting for completeness (§16.2's "what slabs are, and are not" Note becomes a Rationale with expanded content — both labels are non-normative under R-CNF-01, so this carries no fidelity consequence) and one relocation judged fully EQUIVALENT (the preface's "how to read this document" Note moves out of its blockquote into plain prose at the end of §1, trimmed of one sentence whose two component facts are both independently stated elsewhere in both editions).

I opened and closed several other candidates without finding a loss: §2.3's detailed enumeration of which writer obligations are "conduct, not output" compresses to one generic sentence in B, but I confirmed each of the five named cases (§9.2's barriers, §6.3's ignore-lane rule, §6.2's pre-trailer gap, §20.3 step 4's fixed-declaration bar, §10.3/§18.3's targeting advice) is still stated, word for word or near enough, at its own home section in B — a relocation, not a loss. I also checked a term-definition change in §3.1 ("every tile of a layer is addressed" in A becomes explicitly generation-qualified in B) and confirmed the generation-dependence is already fully entailed by A's own §11.2/§20.3 text, so B's version is a legitimate clarification rather than an undecided addition. A consistent four-place cross-reference change (§7.1 → §7.3, citing where a user-metadata record's extent is governed) was checked and is a citation correction, not a content change.

I reached every one of the 24 numbered sections and all 8 appendices; none were skipped. Appendices C, E and F produced no difference at all after de-wrapping. The register tables in §21.2–§21.6 that I spot-checked in detail (beyond what the mechanical checker already covers) were byte-for-byte identical between editions.

evidence.sweeps_run: grep -n '^#' on both files (full heading outlines, compared exhaustively, not sampled) found the §3.3 gap and the §2/§3 reorder. grep -n '^> **(Note|Example|Rationale)' on both files found 94 vs 90 labelled blocks; every one paired by fingerprint and file order, logged in scratch/sweep-a-to-b/a-blocks-full.txt and b-blocks-full.txt. diff -u on all ~115 de-wrapped per-subsection file pairs (dewrap.py + splitsec.py, both written to scratch/sweep-a-to-b/): 97 pairs produced a hunk, all 97 read in file order in the combined diffs-all.txt (1711 lines); 18 pairs were byte-identical post-dewrap, confirmed clean. Targeted grep -n controls run against both whole files for: R-ENC-15 (6 hits each), R-SER-04 (consistent relocation), conduct (5 A / 5 B), ignore-lane (17 A / 17 B), pre-trailer (10 A / 9 B, one paraphrase confirmed equivalent), R-MTA-10 (7 A / 7 B), 'not such a ground' (1 A / 0 B — this is swab-05), 'load-bearing|independent of Part II|cannot decode' (3 A / 2 B — this is swab-03), 'unusability|implementation technique' (3 A / 2 B — this is swab-02), F14 cross-reference contexts (3 A / 2 B — this is swab-01). Keyword-frequency counts for MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY, REQUIRED, SHALL over both whole de-wrapped documents, then narrowed per-subsection via a loop over every matched file pair to localize the one SHOULD discrepancy to §6.3.
evidence.derived_numbers: 94 (A) and 90 (B) labelled-block counts, reconciled as 94 − 5 dropped + 1 added = 90, matching exactly — I verified this arithmetic against the actual pairing rather than asserting it. The §21.8 vector-coverage figures ('120 conditions over 277 instances') are stated identically in both editions, so not a quantity I derived myself, only confirmed unchanged. In swab-06 I checked that B's new '19 MiB at a million tiles and 190 MiB at ten million' figures follow from A's own stated 20-bytes-per-entry fact (§15.1, unchanged in both editions) times 1,000,000 and 10,000,000 respectively (≈19.07 MiB and ≈190.7 MiB), confirming the new Rationale's numbers are a legitimate derivation from A's own text and not a fabricated addition. The MUST/MUST NOT/MAY/REQUIRED/SHALL counts (220/220, 78/78, 57/57, 1/1, 2/2) and the SHOULD counts (48 vs 49, later localized to §6.3's 2-vs-3 in that one subsection) were all produced by my own grep -o | wc -l commands against the de-wrapped files, not read off any pre-existing figure in either document.

Closed: read each of the five named sections in B directly and found the 'this is conduct, not a file-conformance violation' statement present at each one's own home section, word for word or near enough — a relocation, confirmed by direct quotation match, not a loss. Opened: does §3.1's generation-qualified 'addressed tile' definition in B (versus A's unqualified 'every tile of a layer is addressed') decide something new about geometry changing across generations? evidence.confidence_empty: Where I found little or nothing, I ran a control to make sure the absence was real rather than a blind spot in my method: for Appendices C, E and F, which produced zero diff hunks after de-wrapping, I did not just trust an empty diff output — I confirmed the per-subsection .dw files for those appendices existed and were non-empty on both sides (so 'no hunk' meant byte-identical content, not a missing file that diff silently skipped). For the register tables in §21.2, §21.5 and §21.6, which the brief says the mechanical checker already compares and which I was told not to re-diff, I nonetheless spot-read the full table text in both editions at the points where the surrounding prose changed, specifically to catch a table row quietly edited alongside a prose rewrite, and found none. For the keyword-frequency check, an all-zero result (MUST, MUST NOT, MAY, REQUIRED, SHALL every one exactly equal between editions) is itself the control: a rewrite this size with zero drift in five of seven modal-verb counts is what let me trust the one non-zero result (SHOULD, off by one) was worth chasing down rather than noise, and chasing it down did resolve it to a specific, explainable, non-substantive sentence.

findings.location_a: §2.3, trailing Note after the R-CNF-13 paragraph
findings.title: Worked F14/F5/F15 cross-major reach illustration dropped, no replacement
findings.detail: A's Note walks three concrete register rows to show that the cross-major 'reach' test is about the invariant a check asserts, not the bytes it reads: F14 reaches despite checksumming bytes a future major may redefine (it only asserts the CRC-32C invariant); F5 does not reach despite being about the physical file size (because the 128-byte floor it asserts is derived from format-major-1-specific facts); F15 does not reach despite its Governing rule cell citing R-CNT-24 (the specific bytes it zero-checks are inside the 48 a future major may redefine). B replaces the whole Note with one sentence, '§21.2 lists the rows that reach.' The list itself (F8, F14, F6, both of F1's instances) is identical, verbatim, in §21.2 of both editions, so no file's accept/reject verdict differs — but an implementer trying to apply R-CNF-13 to a *new*, unlisted condition has, in A, a worked method with three contrastive examples, and in B, nothing but the pre-computed answer for the existing rows.
findings.quotation_a: **Note.** The test is the invariant a condition violates, not the fields it reads, and three rows show why the distinction carries the weight. §21.2's F14 reaches although the bytes it checksums include fields a future major may redefine: it consumes them as CRC input and asserts only `[R-CNT-24]`'s CRC-32C at F − 4 over [F − 64, F − 4). F5 does not reach although its subject is the physical file size, which no major can redefine: the 128-byte floor it asserts is derived from a directory of at least 4 bytes at an offset of at least 16 and a 64-aligned F (`[R-CNT-27]`), and those are format major 1's. F15 does not reach although its Governing rule cell cites `[R-CNT-24]`: the trailer bytes it requires be zero are inside the 48 that rule lets a future major redefine.
findings.quotation_b: absent — the paragraph ends instead with: "Every other condition concerns a structure this document defines for format major 1 alone ... §21.2 lists the rows that reach. `[R-CNF-13]`"
findings.byte_level_rationale: §21.2's own enumeration of which rows reach (F8, F14, F6, both F1 instances, and no other row) is word-for-word identical in both editions, so any implementation or vector built from either edition reaches the same conclusion for every existing condition; what differs is only the worked derivation that would let someone extend the test to a condition the register does not already enumerate.

findings.quotation_a: **Note.** "Reject" prescribes the scope of unusability, not user interface: how failure is reported is implementation technique.

#### 3.3 Container and array model

> **Note.** Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction: no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode — that independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20.

findings.detail: A's §2.3 enumerates the grounds on which a verifier reports *cannot establish* and then explicitly carves out one case: a user-metadata document under an experimental-range encoding is *not* such a ground, because no content rule attaches there so nothing is left unchecked and certification is unaffected (R-MTA-10), while encoding 0 and a reserved value remain violations under R1. findings.quotation_a: A user-metadata document under an experimental-range encoding — one this specification does not assign and a conforming file can carry (§21.6) — is not such a ground: no content rule attaches there, so nothing is left unchecked, and certification is unaffected (`[R-MTA-10]`); encoding 0 and a reserved value are violations (§21.5, R1).
findings.quotation_b: A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports *cannot establish* (`[R-CNF-11]`), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter (`[R-COD-11]`, §17.4), it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations (`[R-ERR-04]`, `[R-SER-05]`, `[R-SER-08]`), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document (`[R-MTA-09]`).
findings.byte_level_rationale: §21.6's own table row for an experimental-range user-metadata encoding ("the file is conforming ... a verifier certifies, reporting the record it ignored") is unchanged, verbatim, in both editions, so the actual verdict a verifier reaches is identical either way; what is missing from B is the explicit sentence that would tell a reader assembling the cannot-establish list from §21.6 alone that this particular case is excluded, rather than requiring them to cross-check the table row.

findings.title: New Rationale in §15.4 adds two worked MiB figures A never states
findings.detail: B inserts a Rationale explaining why the tile index is segmented (bounding what a reader must verify to use one entry) and, in doing so, states two new concrete figures for a hypothetical unsegmented design: "about 19 MiB at a million tiles and 190 MiB at ten million." Both numbers follow by straightforward arithmetic from facts A already states elsewhere unchanged (20 bytes per index entry, §15.1), so the derivation is A's own text, but A itself never writes these figures or this Rationale.
findings.quotation_a: absent
findings.quotation_b: **Rationale.** Segments bound what a reader verifies to use one entry. Under a single CRC over the whole entry array, verify-before-use (§8.2) would oblige a remote reader to fetch the entire index to use any entry: about 19 MiB at a million tiles and 190 MiB at ten million. With one CRC per 2¹⁶ entries and a CRC over the CRC array, a reader fetches the array and the one segment holding its entry, never more than 1.25 MiB plus the array at any layer scale, and both ranges follow from the layer record alone. Segments are not an option a writer takes or declines...
findings.byte_level_rationale: Rationale blocks are non-normative under R-CNF-01; the new figures explain an already-decided design (segmentation, unchanged and normative in both editions) rather than deciding anything new, so no implementation's bytes or accept/reject verdict is affected.

findings.location_a: §16.2, block labelled "Note — what slabs are, and are not"
findings.location_b: §16.2, same position, now labelled "Rationale" with expanded content
findings.title: Labelled-block relabelling: slab-scope Note becomes a Rationale, with new explanatory material added
findings.detail: The block explaining what a slab guarantees (contiguity) versus what it does not (rectangular-window locality) changes its label from Note to Rationale between editions, and gains new sentences on why a reader benefits from the contiguity promise (one-range fetch, buffer sizing before touching the index) and an explicit statement of A_slab's role (alignment for direct I/O at a run's start). Both labels are non-normative under R-CNF-01, so the relabelling itself changes nothing normatively; logged because the charter asks for every label change between Note/Example/Rationale to be reported, and because the added material, like swab-06, is new prose not present in A.
findings.quotation_a: **Note — what slabs are, and are not.** A slab guarantees *contiguity*: consecutive disk ordinals occupy consecutive bytes. Which tiles are ordinal-consecutive is the linearization field's job (§11.4); under row-major, a run is a band along the last-declared dimension. ... With A_slab = 1 a slab is contiguity-only — the right declaration for remote range coalescing with no direct-I/O alignment need.
findings.quotation_b: **Rationale.** A slab promises one thing, contiguity: within a run, consecutive disk ordinals occupy consecutive bytes. A reader that wants a run can therefore fetch it as one range ... A_slab adds alignment for direct I/O at each run's start; with A_slab = 1 a slab is contiguity alone, the right declaration for coalescing remote range requests when no direct-I/O alignment is needed.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both Note and Rationale are non-normative under R-CNF-01 in both editions; the underlying normative slab rules (R-SLB-01 through R-SLB-05), unchanged elsewhere, are what actually governs byte layout, so no implementation differs.
