result.disclosure: A message labelled "user request" was relayed above this brief, reading only "Go." Per the brief's own instructions this carries no task content, needs no reconciliation with the brief, and does not widen the access rule; nothing else was placed in my context before I began. I worked strictly within the ACCESS RULE: only the two named tarn.md files were opened; no other path was read; no directory was listed except my own scratch and out directories, which I created myself.
result.summary: I compared A (scratch/cleanroom/editions/a/tarn.md, 5004 lines) against B (spec/tarn.md, 4810 lines). Both are hard-wrapped with "> " blockquote prefixes, so I normalized whitespace per paragraph/blockquote block before diffing, and verified every apparent zero with a control search before relying on it. A requirement-ID sweep found exactly the same 163 distinct IDs cited in both editions, none added, none removed, ruling out any requirement being invented or silently dropped. A per-ID citation-count comparison found 15 IDs with a differing number of citations; reading every citing paragraph for each, all 15 were explained by section reorganization (content moved to a different subsection and cited once there instead of twice, or vice versa), never by a rule disappearing. I then ran a heading-aligned, word-count-ranked diff over all 129 matched headings (B keeps every A heading except moving §2 Conformance after §3 Terminology, a pure reorder) and manually read the roughly 15 largest deltas in full. These resolved to: (a) the project's own "re-wrap, no word changed" punctuation passes (em-dash to comma/colon), confirmed by word-for-word diff; (b) legitimate relocation of identical or equivalent sentences to a more natural home section, content still fully present and discoverable from B alone, confirmed by reading the new home section; or (c) a new Rationale/Note in B that derives directly from a definition A's own unchanged text already states without alternative, so not a new decision. I built six concrete constructions to bytes (a reserved-range MU=1 record type; a cross-layer extent overlap; an oversized pre-trailer pad; an appender changing a stored tile's codec without a fresh file_id; a structurally-rejected tile-index entry inside a slab run; and the Appendix B §7.1-vs-§7.3 citation for the user-metadata extent minimum) and in every case both editions license or bar the same bytes and reach the same accept/reject/verdict, because the governing normative sentence is either byte-identical or relocated-but-intact. The one genuine, unrelocated omission I found is §3.3's Note in A ("Part I is independent of Part II by construction... appenders... operate on files whose layers they cannot decode... load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20"), which has no counterpart anywhere in B (grepped "Part II", "cannot decode", "load-bearing", "independent of Part" — only one unrelated hit). I did not carry this to a byte-level construction because it states no testable rule of its own: the fact it explains (an updater need not decode Part II content) is already established in both editions by §2.3's definition of "Conforming updater" ("without necessarily understanding all of its content") and by §20's actual obligations, which never condition on decoding sample data in either edition. So it is a real content loss but not one with byte-level consequence, and I report it as such.

evidence.sweeps_run: grep -oE for requirement IDs across both files, sorted/uniqued (163 vs 163, zero diff) and then sorted/uniqued with counts (15 IDs with differing counts, all individually traced); grep for every heading line (^#{2,4} ) in both files to build an aligned section map (one heading, §3.3, found only in A); a Python script that split both files into heading-delimited blocks, normalized whitespace within each paragraph/blockquote, and flagged the 97 of 129 matched headings with any block-level textual difference, which I then word-counted and ranked to prioritize review; targeted control greps for exact phrases from suspected-missing sentences (e.g. 'worked numeric example', 'paired conformance vector', 'Appendix B' near constants, 'name is structural', 'Part II', 'cannot decode', 'load-bearing', 'independent of Part', 'R-SER-04') run against the full text of whichever edition I suspected was missing content, each returning the hit count (zero for the five phrases confirmed genuinely absent from B, nonzero as a sanity check against the same phrases in A).
evidence.derived_numbers: None of my own arithmetic was load-bearing to a finding; the only 'derived' quantities were word counts per extracted section (wc -w) used purely to rank which of 129 sections to read first, not cited as evidence of anything substantive, and line-number arithmetic to locate each edition's own heading boundaries (e.g., confirming that A's extent_length-≥-5 rule falls within A's own §7.1 span [971,1009) and B's falls within B's own §7.3 span [927,978), which is what resolved the Appendix B §7.1-vs-§7.3 citation difference as a correct, edition-relative cross-reference rather than an error).
evidence.rejected_candidates: (1) §2.3's 541-word delta, the largest in the corpus: opened on the hypothesis that B dropped three enumerated conduct-only-writer-obligation cases; closed because all three (ignore-lane-bit, pre-trailer-pad, §20.3-step-4 fixed-declaration bar) are independently and identically stated at their own home sections (§6.2, §6.3, §20.3), confirmed by reading each home section in both editions. (2) §21.6's new closing paragraph in B (verifier 'cannot establish' grounds): opened as a possible addition; closed because it is the identical sentence relocated verbatim from A's §2.3 'Conforming verifier' bullet, found by matching the exact wording and requirement citations at its new address. (3) New Rationale blocks at §15.4 and §16.2: opened as possible ADDITIONs (B deciding something A leaves open); closed as EQUIVALENT because each new sentence is a direct derivation from a definition A's own unchanged text states without alternative (§15.4's fixed 2^16-entry segment boundary; §16.2's already-normative R-SLB rules). (4) R-ENC-15's citation-count drop (9 to 8): opened as a possible lost duplicate-name rule; closed because the single dropped citation is a non-normative forward-reference aid in §4.7, and the actual rule (register rows F4, L9) is byte-identical in both editions' §21. (5) §4.7's three dropped closing sentences ('A name is structural...', 'worked numeric example...', 'Appendix B'): opened via control grep showing zero hits in B; closed as EQUIVALENT/out-of-scope rather than LOSS because (a) 'name is structural' is a fully redundant consequence of a sentence both editions retain two sentences earlier ('version_minor is the only descriptive field... every other field is structural'), and (b) the remaining sentences are claims about the document's own presentation conventions, not about the format, so their absence changes no implementer's bytes or verdicts. (6) Appendix G and §24's large word-count deltas: opened as possible content loss given their size; closed after a full diff showed every difference was an em-dash-to-comma/colon substitution, zero words added or removed, consistent with the project's own 're-wrapped, no word changed' editorial passes visible in its git history.
evidence.confidence_empty: The zero-diff requirement-ID sweep (163 of 163, identical set) is the strongest control I have that no requirement was invented or deleted outright; it would have caught a dropped or added rule ID even if I had read no prose at all. For every phrase I concluded was genuinely absent from the other edition (the five in rejected-candidate 5, plus §3.3's Note), I ran the control grep against the edition where I expected to find it and got nonzero hits first, confirming the search itself was capable of finding the phrase before trusting its zero against the other edition. I did not find any area where my sweeps came back empty without such a control; the one finding I report (§3.3's Note) survived exactly this control.

findings.title: B drops A's Part I/Part II independence note with no relocation found
findings.detail: A's §3.3 is a single Note explaining that Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction, and that this independence is 'load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20' because it lets appenders and rewriters operate on layers they cannot decode. An implementer working from B alone would therefore build the same appender behavior as one working from A, since nothing in B's normative text asks an updater to decode sample payloads it does not need to touch. result.summary:
I compared edition A (scratch/cleanroom/editions/a/tarn.md) and edition B (spec/tarn.md) at the passages behind all seven divergences in slate A's mechanical match. For each, I grepped the cited requirement ID(s) in both files, opened the full paragraph(s) or table rows both takers quoted plus any neighboring text the question turns on, and checked whether the two editions decide the question the same way.

Result: all seven divergences are EQUIVALENT. In every case the governing sentence(s) are the same text in both editions, with only the cosmetic, systematic rewrap this project's readability pass applies throughout (an em-dash-bracketed aside in A becomes a comma- or semicolon-bracketed one in B, or a mid-sentence aside moves to a trailing sentence) — never a changed quantifier, scope, number, or outcome class.

No LOSS, ADDITION, or REPORTER_ERROR survived: neither taker misread a passage that decides its question, since each taker's quoted text appears, and decides the question the same way, in both editions.

findings.title: Packed-bool pad-bit fill rule and decoded-size formula are identical; both compute 00 00 F0

For P=20 with all 20 real values false and fill=true, both editions' rules yield bytes 0-1 = 0x00 (real positions 0-15), and byte 2 = 0xF0 (real positions 16-19 false in the low nibble, pad bits 4-7 set to the true fill in the high nibble).

findings.quotation_b: Every pad bit (§14.3) MUST carry the plane's channel's fill bit.

findings.title: Codec-4 (lz4) 0x7E000000 decoded-size cap and its reject-layer, declaration-only framing are identical

findings.quotation_b: Writers MUST NOT declare this codec for a layer any of whose addressed tiles' decoded size exceeds 0x7E000000 bytes, the block format's practical interoperability bound, and a reader MUST treat such a declaration as a validity error at layer scope, checkable from declarations alone.

findings.title: Dimension/channel shared-name permission under R-ENC-15 is stated identically

findings.quotation_b: For a type the updater implements that this specification does not register, the definition it implements the type from supplies the flags, and the stored bits never do.

result.disclosure: A relayed "user request" (the single word "Go") appeared prepended above the computed brief; per the brief's own framing this is the launcher's message to the orchestrator, already carried out before this session was spawned, not a task for this session, and it did not widen the access rule — the access rule was followed as the two named files only (edition A at scratch/cleanroom/editions/a/tarn.md and edition B at spec/tarn.md), opened by name via grep/sed, with no directory listed.
result.summary: All six flagged divergences (q02, q03, q04, q11, q12, q13) were read at the takers' cited sections in both edition A (scratch/cleanroom/editions/a/tarn.md) and edition B (spec/tarn.md), plus the §4.6 and §2.3 passages those questions turn on. In every case the two editions state the identical rule, quantifier, table row, and outcome at the point the question decides on: q02's R-CNT-09 suffix-window containment test and the trailer-layout constants; q03's R-CNT-15 MU-gate and §10.3's experimental-range conformance point; q04's R-CNT-04 residency test; q11's §19.1 step 4 raw-byte-first duplicate-name rule; q12's §20.3 step 4 permitted-vs-fixed declaration lists; and q13's §15.3 structural reject-tile row plus §20.5's two-disposition sentence for R-WRT-06. The observed differences between A and B at each passage were limited to sentence-boundary rewording, paragraph breaks, or single-word synonym swaps (e.g. "govern notwithstanding" vs "override" in §15.3's lead sentence; "no other prefix" vs "no further prefix" in §6.1's Note) that change no rule, scope, quantifier, or outcome. Correspondingly, both blind takers gave the same decision for every sub-question, just phrased differently, with no case where one taker's stated reasoning track a sentence the other edition lacks or contradicts. One citation-level oddity surfaced in q03: the A-side taker labelled a point with "§2.3 [R-CNF-03]" where the content it describes (file conformance as a pure predicate on bytes) is actually R-CNF-02's role in both editions alike, R-CNF-03 being the adjacent "conforming reader" rule a few lines below it. This is a citation slip internal to that taker's own apparatus — both editions place R-CNF-02 and R-CNF-03 identically — and it did not change that taker's stated answer to any of (a)-(d), so it is noted as a sub-observation under q03 rather than raised as its own REPORTER_ERROR finding, since it reflects neither a text divergence between editions nor an answer-changing misreading. All six findings are therefore EQUIVALENT: differences of wording or sentence structure that decide nothing differently and would not cause an implementation built from B alone to emit different bytes or reach a different accept/reject verdict than one built from A alone.

findings.title: Suffix-window containment test and region arithmetic are identical in A and B
findings.detail: Both editions give the identical containment rule ('if the fetched buffer contains the directory region, request 2 is unnecessary') and identical trailer-layout fields (dir_offset, dir_length) feeding the region formula [dir_offset, dir_offset+dir_length). Applying the question's numbers to either edition yields the same region [1998900,1999020) and the same 'no, second request required' verdict, since 1998900 (region start) is earlier than 1999000 (window start) in both. The two takers' answers differ only in which side of the inequality they state first ('begins after 1,998,900' vs 'begins 100 bytes earlier'), not in content.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MAY instead speculatively fetch a suffix window in one request and use containment: if the fetched buffer contains the directory region, request 2 is unnecessary.
findings.quotation_b: A reader MAY instead speculatively fetch a suffix window in one request and use containment: if the fetched buffer contains the directory region, request 2 is unnecessary.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Edition A and B state the identical containment test and the identical trailer field definitions feeding it; an implementation built from either alone computes the same region, the same containment check, and reaches the same yes/no and byte range on this file.

findings.title: Experimental-range classification and MU-gate outcomes for type 0x8123 match in A and B
findings.detail: Both editions' §10.2 table place 0x8123 (>= 0x8000) in the experimental range; both §7.2's R-CNT-15 state the identical MU-gate (MU=1 reject-file, MU=0 ignore-record) and both state the experimental-range emission is conforming because §10.3's prohibition binds writer conduct, not the bytes (R-CNF-02), while a reserved-range emission is itself a violation. The A-side taker cited this last point as '§2.3 [R-CNF-03]'; reading A's own §2.3 shows R-CNF-02 is the file-conformance-predicate rule that content actually belongs to, and R-CNF-03 is the adjacent, distinct 'conforming reader' rule (no subset profiles) a few lines below it — the same split exists identically in B. This is a labelling slip inside that taker's own citation, not a difference between what A and B say, and it did not change the taker's stated answers to (a)-(d), which match B's taker on all four points.
findings.quotation_a: An unknown record type at file scope: MU = 1 → reject-file; MU = 0 → ignore-record. ... a record type from the experimental range is conforming ... while one from the reserved range is a value this specification has not assigned — emitting it is a violation.
findings.quotation_b: A record at file scope whose type the reader does not implement is governed by its stored MU bit: MU = 1 is reject-file, and MU = 0 is ignore-record. That rule is about what a reader does, not about whether the file is valid. A record type from the experimental range is conforming: §10.3's prohibition binds the writer's conduct, not the bytes (`[R-CNF-02]`).
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both editions fix the same classification (experimental), the same two MU-gate outcomes, and the same conforming/violation split between experimental and reserved ranges, so an implementation built from either alone reaches the same four verdicts on this record.

findings.title: Residency-governed front-block check is stated identically in A and B
findings.detail: Both editions state the same residency test: a reader whose open leaves bytes [0,16) resident MUST verify the block by byte equality and MUST reject-file on mismatch, while one that would need a further range request MAY defer or omit the check — explicitly naming residency, not transport, as the deciding concept in both. Applied to the question, both editions give a memory-mapped local reader the detect/reject-file obligation and give a trailer-anchored remote reader no such obligation.
findings.quotation_a: A reader whose open leaves bytes [0, 16) resident ... MUST verify the full block by byte equality before other processing, and MUST treat any mismatch as reject-file. A reader that would have to issue a further range request to obtain those bytes MAY defer or omit the check.
findings.quotation_b: A reader whose open leaves bytes [0, 16) resident (e.g. a local file read whole, a memory mapping, a speculative suffix window that reached offset 0, or any transport already holding them) MUST verify the full block by byte equality before other processing, and MUST treat any mismatch as reject-file. A reader that would have to issue a further range request to obtain those bytes MAY defer or omit the check.
findings.byte_level_rationale: The residency test and its two outcomes (mandatory reject-file vs no obligation) are stated identically in both editions, so an implementation built from either alone handles the memory-mapped and trailer-anchored-remote cases the same way.

findings.title: Raw-byte-first duplicate-name determination, independent of name validity, matches in A and B
findings.detail: Both editions state that uniqueness is decided first and over raw name bytes regardless of each name's own well-formedness, citing R-ENC-13's byte-comparison rule for why validity is irrelevant to the duplicate check, and both conclude two byte-identical name fields are a duplicate (reject-file) even when neither name is independently valid (here, both contain the embedded 0x00 control byte).
findings.quotation_a: Uniqueness is decided first, and over the raw name bytes whether or not each name is itself well-formed — `[R-ENC-13]` makes name comparison a byte comparison, which needs no valid name — so two layers whose name fields are byte-identical are a duplicate even when neither name is valid.
findings.quotation_b: Uniqueness is decided first, and over the raw name bytes whether or not each name is itself well-formed, because `[R-ENC-13]` makes name comparison a byte comparison, which needs no valid name; so two layers whose name fields are byte-identical are a duplicate even when neither name is valid.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both editions fix the identical sequencing (uniqueness before validity) and the identical byte-comparison basis, so an implementation built from either alone reaches the same reject-file verdict on two byte-identical, independently-invalid names.

findings.title: Permitted extent growth vs fixed codec, and the rewrite-or-new-layer alternative, match in A and B
findings.detail: Both editions list a dimension extent's growth (not shrinkage) among the changes an appender commit MAY make to a layer that stores a tile, and both fix the codec (with the filter, layout, linearization, index encoding, etc.) as unchangeable for as long as the layer stores a tile, with the identical consequence sentence that changing it requires a new layer or a rewrite re-declaring it under a fresh file_id.
findings.quotation_a: a dimension extent MAY grow, and MUST NOT shrink ... Every other declaration is fixed for as long as the layer stores a tile: ... the codec and the filter ... A commit MUST NOT change one of these; the change is a new layer, or a rewrite that re-declares it under a fresh file_id.
findings.quotation_b: a dimension extent MAY grow, and MUST NOT shrink; ... Every other declaration is fixed for as long as the layer stores a tile: the layout, the linearization and the index encoding, the codec and the filter, ... A commit MUST NOT change one of these; the change is a new layer, or a rewrite that re-declares it under a fresh file_id
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both editions permit exactly the same change (extent growth) and fix exactly the same declarations (codec included) with the identical two-way alternative stated for changing a fixed one, so an implementation built from either alone accepts (a) and rejects (b) identically and requires the same remedial operation.

findings.title: The two-disposition rule for a structurally malformed index entry under regeneration matches in A and B
findings.detail: Both editions classify offset=sentinel/length-not-sentinel as a structural reject-tile row (R-IDX-03) giving the entry no stored extent, and both state the rewriter's regeneration step (R-WRT-06) leaves exactly two dispositions — drop the layer, or refuse — explicitly because the entry can neither be reproduced nor have a replacement invented, foreclosing 'carry forward unchanged' as a third option in identical language.
findings.quotation_a: `[R-WRT-06]` then leaves it two disposals, since it can neither reproduce the entry nor invent a replacement: drop the layer, which §20.4's table licenses ..., or refuse.
findings.quotation_b: `[R-WRT-06]` then leaves it two disposals, since it can neither reproduce the entry nor invent a replacement: drop the layer, which §20.4's table licenses and whose loss the rewriter SHOULD report as that table says, or refuse.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both editions name the identical two dispositions and the identical reasoning foreclosing a third, so an implementation built from either alone has exactly the same two available outcomes for this entry during region regeneration.

quizDivergences.title: Slate A quiza-07: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: A planar bool channel declares fill = true (the byte 0x01). One of its addressed, fully-stored tiles has exactly P = 20 sample positions, every one of them a real (non-edge-padding) array position, and every one of those 20 real values is false. What are the tile's three decoded bytes, in hexadecimal, in stored order?
FROM A: 00 00 F0 [high] cites §14.3 (R-SER-03); §14.5 (R-SER-05)
FROM B: 0x00, 0x00, 0xF0 [high] cites §14.3 (R-SER-03); §14.5 (R-SER-05)
A's reasoning: 20 real values all false fill bytes 0 and 1 and low nibble of byte 2 with zeros; fill=true sets the 4 pad bits (bits 4-7 of byte 2) to 1, giving 0xF0.
B's reasoning: Decoded size=ceil(20/8)=3 bytes. Bytes 0-1 hold values 0-15, all false=0x00 each. Byte 2 holds real values 16-19 (false) in bits 0-3 and pad bits 4-7 (P mod 8=4), which must carry the fill bit (true=1), giving 0b11110000=0xF0.
quizDivergences.quotation_a: Every pad bit (§14.3) MUST carry the plane's channel's fill bit.
quizDivergences.quotation_b: Every pad bit (§14.3) MUST carry the plane's channel's fill bit.

quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: During one region-read request against an interleaved layer, a reader has already returned decoded values for several tiles earlier in that same request, then reaches a tile whose segment CRC fails verification. Per R-RDR-04: (a) what happens to the values already returned earlier in this same request, and (b) what happens to this layer for any later request in the same reader's session?
FROM A: (a) they stand; (b) the layer is barred from all further service for the rest of the session [high] cites §19.4 step 8 (R-RDR-04)
FROM B: (a) stand unaffected; (b) barred from all further service for the rest of the session [high] cites §19.4 step 3 (R-RDR-04); §2.4 outcome-class table (reject-layer)
A's reasoning: A segment-CRC (index-chain) failure is a layer-scope failure under R-IDX-04; R-RDR-04 fixes that it bars all further service from that layer while not retracting values already returned earlier in the same request.
B's reasoning: A segment-CRC failure is an index-chain (layer-scope) failure. R-RDR-04 and the reject-layer outcome definition make the bar prospective only: earlier-returned values in this request stand, and the layer is barred from all further service, i.e. no later request in the same session may be served from it.
quizDivergences.quotation_a: A failure inside the same request that takes layer scope instead ... bars the request's remaining entries and all further service from the layer; the bar is prospective, so values the reader has already returned under §19.2's timing stand

QUESTION: A file's total size is 2,000,000 bytes. Its trailer gives dir_offset = 1,998,900 and dir_length = 120. A remote reader's first request speculatively fetches the suffix window [1,999,000, 2,000,000) (1000 bytes). State the directory region's exact byte range, and say whether this window satisfies the containment test that would make a second request unnecessary (yes/no), with the one-sentence arithmetic reason.
FROM A: [1998900, 1999020); no; the window begins at 1,999,000, which is after the directory region's own start at 1,998,900, so the window omits the directory's first 100 bytes and does not contain it. [high] cites §6.2 trailer layout (dir_offset, dir_length); §6.4 [R-CNT-09]

B's reasoning: Region = [1998900, 1998900+120) = [1998900,1999020). Window=[1999000,2000000). Containment requires region_start>=window_start; 1998900<1999000 so containment fails, verified by direct arithmetic.

quizDivergences.title: Slate B quizb-q03: the editions' takers answer differently

QUESTION: A writer emits a top-level record with type value 0x8123. (a) Classify this value as assigned, reserved, or experimental. (b) If a reader does not implement this type and the record's stored MUST_UNDERSTAND bit is 1, what must the reader do, and does the file count as nonconforming on account of this record? (c) Give the same two answers for MUST_UNDERSTAND = 0. (d) Would either emission (MU=1 or MU=0) itself register as a file-conformance violation the way emitting an unassigned reserved-range type value would?
FROM A: (a) experimental; (b) reject-file; not nonconforming; (c) ignore-record; not nonconforming; (d) no [high] cites §10.2 table; §7.2/§10.3 [R-CNT-15]; §2.3 [R-CNF-03]
FROM B: (a) experimental; (b) reject-file, No; (c) ignore-record, No; (d) No [high] cites §10.2 (record type numeric space table); §10.3 (experimental range rules, R-CNF-02); §7.2/R-CNT-15 (MU-bit outcome)
A's reasoning: 0x8123 ≥ 0x8000, so it falls in the experimental range per §10.2's table (assigned 0x0001/0x0002, reserved 0x0003–0x7FFF, experimental ≥0x8000). R-CNT-15 fixes the reader action by MU bit (reject-file / ignore-record) and states explicitly that an experimental-range type is conforming regardless, unlike a reserved-range (unassigned) type, whose emission is itself a violation — answering (d) 'no'.
B's reasoning: 0x8123 >= 0x8000 falls in the experimental range per §10.2's table. R-CNT-15 fixes MU=1 -> reject-file and MU=0 -> ignore-record as reader actions 'about what a reader does, not about whether the file is valid.' §10.3 states explicitly that an experimental-range type's emission is conforming regardless, unlike a reserved-range type, whose emission is itself a violation a verifier must flag — hence (d) is No.

quizDivergences.title: Slate B quizb-q04: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: A local reader memory-maps the whole file, so every byte is resident at open. Bytes [0,8) read as the correct magic, but one byte inside [8,16) is 0x01 instead of 0x00. (a) Must this reader detect the defect, and what outcome follows? (b) Would a remote reader whose open path never fetches bytes [0,16) (anchored at the trailer instead) have the same obligation? Answer (a) and (b) each as a short verdict naming the governing concept.
FROM A: (a) must detect; reject-file; (b) no obligation — governed by residency, not required [high] cites §6.1 [R-CNT-04]
FROM B: (a) reject-file — mandatory, decided by residency: bytes [0,16) are resident in a whole-file memory map; (b) no obligation — decided by residency: the remote reader's open never makes bytes [0,16) resident, so it MAY defer or omit the check [high] cites §6.1 front signature block rule (R-CNT-04)
A's reasoning: A memory-mapped local reader has [0,16) resident at open, so it must verify the whole 16-byte block (including the zero bytes at [8,16)) by equality; the 0x01 byte is a mismatch, giving reject-file. A remote reader anchored at the trailer never needs those bytes and so has no such obligation — the deciding concept is residency, not transport, per R-CNT-04's own text.
B's reasoning: Bytes [8,16) must be zero (front-block layout); one byte is 0x01, a mismatch. Memory-mapped reader has the whole file resident at open, so it must detect and reject-file. A remote reader anchored at the trailer never fetches [0,16), so has no such obligation — both governed by the single concept of residency, R-CNT-04.

QUESTION: Two layer records in one directory have name fields whose raw bytes are both the 3-byte sequence 61 00 62 (which contains the C0 control byte 0x00, itself independently invalid as a name). quizDivergences.title: Slate B quizb-q12: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: A layer currently stores at least one tile, under codec = zstd (3), tile extents (128, 128). A single appender commit attempts, at once: (a) growing one dimension's extent from 1000 to 1200, and (b) changing the layer's codec from zstd (3) to lz4 (4). Taking each change on its own merits as an appender operation (not a rewrite): is change (a) alone permitted? Is change (b) alone permitted? What must a writer that wants change (b) do instead?
FROM A: (a) yes; (b) no; rewrite (re-declare the layer under a fresh file_id) [high] cites §20.3 step 4 [R-WRT-04]
FROM B: (a) Yes; (b) No; declare a new layer, or perform a whole-file rewrite [high] cites §20.3 step 4 (append procedure, permitted vs. fixed declarations, R-WRT-04)
A's reasoning: §20.3 step 4 lists dimension-extent growth among the permitted appender changes to a layer that stores a tile, but fixes codec (and filter) as unchangeable by an appender; changing codec requires either declaring a new layer or performing a rewrite under a fresh file_id.
B's reasoning: §20.3 step 4 lists extent growth as an explicitly permitted change for a layer that stores a tile, and lists codec as one of the declarations fixed for as long as the layer stores a tile, whose change requires a new layer or a rewrite.
quizDivergences.quotation_a: a dimension extent MAY grow, and MUST NOT shrink ... Every other declaration is fixed for as long as the layer stores a tile: ... the codec and the filter ... A commit MUST NOT change one of these; the change is a new layer, or a rewrite that re-declares it under a fresh file_id.
quizDivergences.quotation_b: a dimension extent MAY grow, and MUST NOT shrink... Every other declaration is fixed for as long as the layer stores a tile: the layout, the linearization and the index encoding, the codec and the filter... A commit MUST NOT change one of these; the change is a new layer, or a rewrite that re-declares it under a fresh file_id

quizDivergences.title: Slate B quizb-q13: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: A rewriter is compacting a file and relocating one layer's stored tiles, which requires regenerating that layer's whole tile-index region. One index entry in that region is offset = sentinel, length not sentinel, crc = 0 — a malformed entry that the specification classifies reject-tile on a structural ground. Name the two, and only two, dispositions available to the rewriter for this situation, and say whether "carry this one entry forward unchanged while regenerating the rest of the region" is a third option.
FROM A: drop the layer, refuse; no [high] cites §20.5 [R-WRT-06]; §15.3 [R-IDX-03]
FROM B: [drop the layer, refuse to rewrite]; No [high] cites §15.3 (entry validity, structural reject-tile row, R-IDX-03); §20.5 (rewriting, regenerating a region, R-WRT-06)
A's reasoning: A structurally-malformed entry (offset=sentinel, length not sentinel) has no stored extent to re-point when regenerating the region, so the rewriter can neither reproduce it unchanged nor invent a replacement; the only two disposals the text names are dropping the layer or refusing to rewrite, explicitly foreclosing the 'carry forward unchanged' option.
B's reasoning: The malformed entry (offset=sentinel, length not sentinel, crc=0) matches §15.3's structural reject-tile row, giving it no stored extent to re-point during region regeneration. §20.5 explicitly enumerates exactly two dispositions and explicitly forecloses carrying the entry forward unchanged ('can neither reproduce the entry nor invent a replacement').
quizDivergences.quotation_a: `[R-WRT-06]` then leaves it two disposals, since it can neither reproduce the entry nor invent a replacement: drop the layer, which §20.4's table licenses ..., or refuse.
quizDivergences.quotation_b: R-WRT-06 then leaves it two disposals, since it can neither reproduce the entry nor invent a replacement: drop the layer, which §20.4's table licenses and whose loss the rewriter SHOULD report as that table says, or refuse.

findings.location_a: §17.4, [R-COD-11] (edition A lines 2630-2647, the resolving sentence at 2638-2643)
findings.location_b: §17.4, [R-COD-11] (edition B lines 2509-2524, the resolving sentence at 2516-2521)
findings.title: Walker A misread its own edition: R3's reader-capability answer is present in A, not absent
findings.detail: Both editions state, in the same paragraph as the verifier rule walker A quotes: "For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer (R-COD-03, R-COD-09); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (R-CNF-03)." This directly answers R3 and readera-01's gap: the core-codec-capability case cannot arise for a conforming reader, and the actual in-register case (reserved/experimental codec value) is reject-layer. Walker A's transcript cites exactly this line range (2634-2646) as containing only the verifier rule and concludes "No equivalent text binds an ordinary reader," and its Finding readera-01 repeats the claim as an AMBIGUITY. Walker B, reading the byte-identical sentence in edition B, quoted it correctly and answered R3 as resolved. An implementer who read either edition correctly and completely would reach the same conclusion walker B reached; the divergence in the probe answers is a reading error by walker A on edition A, not a difference between A and B.
findings.quotation_a: For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer (`[R-COD-03]`, `[R-COD-09]`); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (`[R-CNF-03]`). `[R-COD-11]`
findings.quotation_b: For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer (`[R-COD-03]`, `[R-COD-09]`); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (`[R-CNF-03]`). `[R-COD-11]`
findings.byte_level_rationale: An implementation built from either edition alone, read correctly and completely, decides R3 identically (the scenario cannot occur for a conforming reader; the in-register case is reject-layer), so no implementation's bytes or verdicts differ by edition. The divergence recorded in the probe set is between what walker A's implementer would build if it replicated walker A's own misreading versus what a careful reader of either edition would build — not a divergence the text of A vs B causes.

findings.location_b: §2.3, after [R-CNF-13] (edition B line 297, no corresponding Note)
findings.title: Edition B drops A's worked derivation of which register rows 'reach' other format majors
findings.detail: Edition A follows R-CNF-13's abstract 'reach' test with a Note working it by hand over three named rows: F14 reaches (it checksums bytes a future major may redefine, but asserts only R-CNT-24's fixed CRC invariant); F5 does not reach (its 128-byte floor is derived from format-major-1-specific structure sizes, even though its subject, physical file size, is not itself redefinable); F15 does not reach despite its Governing-rule cell citing R-CNT-24 (the specific reserved bytes it checks are inside the part of the trailer R-CNT-24 lets a future major redefine). Edition B has no corresponding Note anywhere in or after §2.3 (confirmed by search: zero hits for this reasoning's key phrases in B's §2.3 region). Both editions' §21.2 opening paragraph states the bottom-line conclusion identically ('Deriving it there yields F8, F14, F6 and both of F1's instances... and no other row'), so no register row's assigned outcome differs between editions — but an implementer of B who wants to understand (or extend) why the test sorts rows this way, rather than take the conclusion on faith, must re-derive A's three-example reasoning from scratch. Walker B's own transcript shows exactly this forced re-derivation happening under R6: 'I checked this because I expected F5 might be a fifth reaches-every-major row... it does not name F5 among the four... I [worked out] this is because R-CNT-27's check needs no byte of the file's content' — independently reconstructing, unprompted, what A's Note simply states.
findings.quotation_a: The test is the invariant a condition violates, not the fields it reads, and three rows show why the distinction carries the weight. §21.2's F14 reaches although the bytes it checksums include fields a future major may redefine: it consumes them as CRC input and asserts only [R-CNT-24]'s CRC-32C at F - 4 over [F - 64, F - 4). F5 does not reach although its subject is the physical file size, which no major can redefine: the 128-byte floor it asserts is derived from a directory of at least 4 bytes at an offset of at least 16 and a 64-aligned F ([R-CNT-27]), and those are format major 1's. F15 does not reach although its Governing rule cell cites [R-CNT-24]: the trailer bytes it requires be zero are inside the 48 that rule lets a future major redefine.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: B's §21.2 opening states the same conclusion (which specific rows reach) in the same words as A's, so every register row's assigned outcome, and hence every byte a conforming implementation accepts or rejects for the current rule set, is identical between editions. The loss is of the worked justification an implementer or future ADR author would need to correctly classify a *new* condition's reach without re-deriving the test from scratch — a loss of determinacy/explanatory support, not of a currently-decided byte-level outcome.

findings.title: Edition A states an explicit derivation linking MU=1-unimplemented-type to the experimental range; B omits it entirely
findings.detail: Edition A's Conforming-reader definition states: a reader must accept every conforming file, 'carrying no top-level record of a type it does not implement with MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 -- in a conforming file such a type is necessarily from the experimental range, since a reserved-range type carrying MU = 1 is itself a violation -- and none of whose values exceeds the minimum guarantees of section 21's limits table (section 21.9's R-ERR-04 governs a refusal on that last ground; section 21.6's closing paragraph names the other two).' Edition B's corresponding sentence reads only: 'carrying no top-level record of a type it does not implement with MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 and none of whose values exceeds the minimum guarantees of section 21's limits table (section 21.9).' Both the italicized derivation clause and the citation breakdown are absent from B and are not restated anywhere else in B (confirmed by exhaustive grep with positive controls). An implementer building a reader strictly from B's section 2.3 alone, without separately combining F35/F36 from the register, would not have this inference spelled out at the point of the acceptance obligation; one building from A's section 2.3 would. However, the underlying rule the derivation rests on -- F36, that emitting any reserved-range top-level record type is itself a violation whatever its MU bit -- is present, identically worded, in both editions' registers (section 21.2), so the same conclusion remains fully and independently derivable from B's own text. This is why neither walk's probe V2 answer actually diverged because of it: walker B reached the identical verdict via section 7.2, section 21.2's F35/F36 rows, and section 21.6's two-structural-cases paragraph instead.

findings.quotation_b: carrying no top-level record of a type it does not implement with MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 and none of whose values exceeds the minimum guarantees of section 21's limits table (section 21.9)
