The list itself (F8, F14, F6, both of F1's instances) is identical, verbatim, in §21.2 of both editions, so no file's accept/reject verdict differs — but an implementer trying to apply R-CNF-13 to a *new*, unlisted condition has, in A, a worked method with three contrastive examples, and in B, nothing but the pre-computed answer for the existing rows.
findings.quotation_a: **Note.** The test is the invariant a condition violates, not the fields it reads, and three rows show why the distinction carries the weight. §21.2's F14 reaches although the bytes it checksums include fields a future major may redefine: it consumes them as CRC input and asserts only `[R-CNT-24]`'s CRC-32C at F − 4 over [F − 64, F − 4). F5 does not reach although its subject is the physical file size, which no major can redefine: the 128-byte floor it asserts is derived from a directory of at least 4 bytes at an offset of at least 16 and a 64-aligned F (`[R-CNT-27]`), and those are format major 1's. F15 does not reach although its Governing rule cell cites `[R-CNT-24]`: the trailer bytes it requires be zero are inside the 48 that rule lets a future major redefine.
findings.quotation_b: absent — the paragraph ends instead with: "Every other condition concerns a structure this document defines for format major 1 alone ... §21.2 lists the rows that reach. `[R-CNF-13]`"
findings.byte_level_rationale: §21.2's own enumeration of which rows reach (F8, F14, F6, both F1 instances, and no other row) is word-for-word identical in both editions, so any implementation or vector built from either edition reaches the same conclusion for every existing condition; what differs is only the worked derivation that would let someone extend the test to a condition the register does not already enumerate.

findings.location_a: §2.4, trailing Note after the R-CNF-12 paragraph
findings.title: Clarifying Note on the scope of the word 'reject' deleted with no replacement
findings.detail: A states explicitly that the outcome-class vocabulary's word 'reject' (reject-file, reject-layer, reject-tile) constrains the scope of unusability a conforming reader must observe, and nothing about how a reader surfaces that to a user or caller — i.e. it is not a UI/API requirement. This sentence is simply gone from B. I grepped both whole documents for 'unusability' and 'implementation technique': in A both phrases occur at two places (this Note and the unrelated §2.1 Note on requirement phrasing discipline), while in B only the §2.1 occurrence survives.
findings.quotation_a: **Note.** "Reject" prescribes the scope of unusability, not user interface: how failure is reported is implementation technique.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: The note bears on how 'reject' should be interpreted by an implementer deciding what counts as satisfying a reject-* obligation (data unusability) versus what is left to implementation choice (error reporting/UI); it does not itself add or remove a MUST/SHOULD, so no implementation built correctly from either edition's MUST-level rules would diverge in bytes emitted or accept/reject verdicts — but B no longer forecloses a stricter (incorrect) reading that 'reject' also prescribes reporting mechanics.

findings.location_a: §3.3 "Container and array model" (the entire subsection, heading included)
findings.location_b: absent — B's §3 has only 3.1 and 3.2; the heading '#### 3.3' does not exist anywhere in edition B
findings.title: Entire §3.3 subsection, on Part I/Part II independence, deleted with no restatement anywhere
findings.detail: A devotes a whole labelled subsection to stating that Part I (the container) is independent of Part II (the array model) by construction — no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads — and that this independence is explicitly 'load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20' (i.e. it is why an appender or a rewriter carrying a layer forward never needs to be able to decode that layer's samples). This entire subsection, including its heading, is absent from B. I grepped B for 'independent of Part II', 'cannot decode', and 'load-bearing' (the last two to catch a paraphrase): the first two return zero hits; 'load-bearing' survives only in two unrelated sentences (§3.1 on declared dimension order, §12.1 on declared channel order), neither of which makes this Part I/Part II claim.
findings.quotation_a:
#### 3.3 Container and array model

> **Note.** Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction: no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode — that independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20.
findings.quotation_b: absent — §3.2 is immediately followed by '### 4. Encoding Conventions' with no intervening subsection
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is a non-normative architectural Note in A (no requirement ID), so it does not itself gate any MUST-level behavior; but it is an explicit cross-section claim ('load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20') that is not restated, even informally, anywhere in B, which is exactly the kind of whole-block disappearance the charter's labelled-block census asks to be reported.

findings.title: Note disambiguating R-ENC-08's scope (flags/packed fields, not sample bit-mapping) dropped
findings.detail: A's §4.4 states the general LSB-first bit-numbering rule (R-ENC-08) and then a Note clarifying that this rule governs 'flags and packed fields generally,' while the mapping of boolean *samples* to bits is a separate rule defined in §14. B drops the Note; I grepped both files for 'R-ENC-08' and found it cited only once in each edition (its own defining paragraph), confirming the disambiguating cross-reference is not picked up anywhere else either.
findings.quotation_a: **Note.** This rule fixes bit numbering in flags and packed fields generally; the mapping of boolean *samples* to bits is defined in §14.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: Lower-severity than the other LOSSes: §14.3 (packed boolean planes), unchanged in both editions, already states its bit order with an explicit '(§4.4)' citation, so the practical linkage between the general rule and its specific application survives without this signpost; no MUST-level behavior is affected either way.

findings.location_b: §21.6, new closing paragraph (where the rest of this content relocated)
findings.title: Negative carve-out — experimental-range user-metadata encoding is not a 'cannot establish' ground — dropped on relocation
findings.detail: A's §2.3 enumerates the grounds on which a verifier reports *cannot establish* and then explicitly carves out one case: a user-metadata document under an experimental-range encoding is *not* such a ground, because no content rule attaches there so nothing is left unchecked and certification is unaffected (R-MTA-10), while encoding 0 and a reserved value remain violations under R1. When B moves the positive-grounds enumeration from §2.3 to a new paragraph at the end of §21.6, this one negative sentence does not travel with it — B's new paragraph lists the five positive grounds and stops.
findings.quotation_a: A user-metadata document under an experimental-range encoding — one this specification does not assign and a conforming file can carry (§21.6) — is not such a ground: no content rule attaches there, so nothing is left unchecked, and certification is unaffected (`[R-MTA-10]`); encoding 0 and a reserved value are violations (§21.5, R1).
findings.quotation_b: A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports *cannot establish* (`[R-CNF-11]`), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter (`[R-COD-11]`, §17.4), it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations (`[R-ERR-04]`, `[R-SER-05]`, `[R-SER-08]`), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document (`[R-MTA-09]`).
findings.byte_level_rationale: §21.6's own table row for an experimental-range user-metadata encoding ("the file is conforming ... a verifier certifies, reporting the record it ignored") is unchanged, verbatim, in both editions, so the actual verdict a verifier reaches is identical either way; what is missing from B is the explicit sentence that would tell a reader assembling the cannot-establish list from §21.6 alone that this particular case is excluded, rather than requiring them to cross-check the table row.

findings.location_a: n/a — no corresponding text anywhere in §15.4
findings.location_b: §15.4, new Rationale block (between the existing "To use" Note and the segment-sentinel-CRC paragraph)
findings.title: New Rationale in §15.4 adds two worked MiB figures A never states
findings.detail: B inserts a Rationale explaining why the tile index is segmented (bounding what a reader must verify to use one entry) and, in doing so, states two new concrete figures for a hypothetical unsegmented design: "about 19 MiB at a million tiles and 190 MiB at ten million." Both numbers follow by straightforward arithmetic from facts A already states elsewhere unchanged (20 bytes per index entry, §15.1), so the derivation is A's own text, but A itself never writes these figures or this Rationale.
findings.quotation_a: absent
findings.quotation_b: **Rationale.** Segments bound what a reader verifies to use one entry. Under a single CRC over the whole entry array, verify-before-use (§8.2) would oblige a remote reader to fetch the entire index to use any entry: about 19 MiB at a million tiles and 190 MiB at ten million. With one CRC per 2¹⁶ entries and a CRC over the CRC array, a reader fetches the array and the one segment holding its entry, never more than 1.25 MiB plus the array at any layer scale, and both ranges follow from the layer record alone. Segments are not an option a writer takes or declines...
findings.byte_level_rationale: Rationale blocks are non-normative under R-CNF-01; the new figures explain an already-decided design (segmentation, unchanged and normative in both editions) rather than deciding anything new, so no implementation's bytes or accept/reject verdict is affected.

findings.location_a: §16.2, block labelled "Note — what slabs are, and are not"
findings.location_b: §16.2, same position, now labelled "Rationale" with expanded content
findings.title: Labelled-block relabelling: slab-scope Note becomes a Rationale, with new explanatory material added
findings.detail: The block explaining what a slab guarantees (contiguity) versus what it does not (rectangular-window locality) changes its label from Note to Rationale between editions, and gains new sentences on why a reader benefits from the contiguity promise (one-range fetch, buffer sizing before touching the index) and an explicit statement of A_slab's role (alignment for direct I/O at a run's start). Both labels are non-normative under R-CNF-01, so the relabelling itself changes nothing normatively; logged because the charter asks for every label change between Note/Example/Rationale to be reported, and because the added material, like swab-06, is new prose not present in A.
findings.quotation_a: **Note — what slabs are, and are not.** A slab guarantees *contiguity*: consecutive disk ordinals occupy consecutive bytes. Which tiles are ordinal-consecutive is the linearization field's job (§11.4); under row-major, a run is a band along the last-declared dimension. ... With A_slab = 1 a slab is contiguity-only — the right declaration for remote range coalescing with no direct-I/O alignment need.
findings.quotation_b: **Rationale.** A slab promises one thing, contiguity: within a run, consecutive disk ordinals occupy consecutive bytes. A reader that wants a run can therefore fetch it as one range ... A_slab adds alignment for direct I/O at each run's start; with A_slab = 1 a slab is contiguity alone, the right declaration for coalescing remote range requests when no direct-I/O alignment is needed.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both Note and Rationale are non-normative under R-CNF-01 in both editions; the underlying normative slab rules (R-SLB-01 through R-SLB-05), unchanged elsewhere, are what actually governs byte layout, so no implementation differs.

findings.location_a: Preface, before "Part 0" (lines 12-20), block labelled "Note. How to read this document."
findings.location_b: End of §1 Introduction, same content as plain bold prose, not a block-quote
findings.title: Preface 'how to read this document' Note moves out of its block-quote into §1's closing paragraph, trimmed of one cross-reference sentence
findings.detail: A's preface carries this guidance as a labelled Note before Part 0 even begins; B moves the rubric sentence and the structural/descriptive field-split sentence into an un-labelled bold paragraph at the very end of §1 (itself non-normative under R-CNF-01 in both editions). The one sentence not carried over — 'Normative requirements carry stable identifiers like [R-IDX-03], and test vectors cite those identifiers rather than prose positions' — has both of its component facts (identifier stability; vectors naming the governing requirement identifier) still stated separately and unchanged in §2.2 and in §24/R-VEC-02 of both editions.
findings.quotation_a: > **Note.** How to read this document. Sections follow a fixed rubric where applicable: purpose, byte-layout table, writer rules, reader rules, error handling, worked examples. ... Normative requirements carry stable identifiers like `[R-IDX-03]`, and test vectors cite those identifiers rather than prose positions.
findings.quotation_b: **How to read this document.** Sections follow a fixed rubric where it applies: purpose, byte-layout table, writer rules, reader rules, error handling, worked examples. On-disk structures are presented as layout tables whose columns suit the structure; §4.7 says what the columns carry and classifies every field as structural or descriptive.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both the Note (A) and §1 generally (B) are non-normative under R-CNF-01 in their own edition, and the one dropped sentence's two facts are independently, unchangedly normative at §2.2 and §24/R-VEC-02 in both editions, so nothing an implementer needs is undecided in B.

findings.location_b: absent (B has no §3.3 heading and no counterpart text anywhere)
findings.title: B drops A's Part I/Part II independence note with no relocation found
findings.detail: A's §3.3 is a single Note explaining that Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction, and that this independence is 'load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20' because it lets appenders and rewriters operate on layers they cannot decode. B has no heading matching '3.3' or 'Container and array model', and I found no paraphrase of the claim anywhere in B (control greps for 'Part II', 'cannot decode', 'load-bearing', 'independent of Part' returned nothing relevant). However, the substance the note explains is independently preserved in both editions elsewhere: §2.3's definition of 'Conforming updater' ('a tool that modifies an existing file... without necessarily understanding all of its content') is present verbatim in both A and B, and §20's actual appender/rewriter obligations never condition on decoding Part II content in either edition. An implementer working from B alone would therefore build the same appender behavior as one working from A, since nothing in B's normative text asks an updater to decode sample payloads it does not need to touch. The loss is of an explanatory/architectural remark that motivates a design choice, not of a rule, carve-out, quantifier, or definition that changes what bytes a conforming implementation emits or what verdict a verifier reaches.
findings.quotation_a: Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction: no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode — that independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: No file construction distinguishes the two editions here: the only testable consequence of the dropped note (an updater may act without decoding a layer's sample payloads) is already fully entailed, in both A and B, by the unchanged 'Conforming updater' definition in §2.3 and by §20.3/§20.4's actual appender and preservation obligations, neither of which requires payload decoding in either edition. I could not construct a file, commit, or verifier run whose accept/reject verdict or emitted bytes differ between an implementation built from A alone versus one built from B alone as a result of this omission.

findings.title: No defined reader behavior for a core-assigned codec/filter the reader lacks
findings.detail: A reader that does not implement a core, assigned codec (e.g. zstd, codec 3) is declared outright not to be a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03]), full stop - this is correct and unambiguous. But the document never says what such software (which still exists and must do something) is permitted to do: may it still serve requests against the file's other layers, or list this layer's declarations without decoding it? For the structurally parallel case of a conforming VERIFIER that cannot execute a codec, the document gives a complete protocol (section 17.4: cannot certify, report 'cannot establish', narrow the claim) - it extends no equivalent courtesy, or even a cross-reference, to an ordinary reader in the same position. Two independently-built, otherwise-conformant-except-for-this-codec readers given the identical file could reasonably diverge: one rejects the whole file (having no stated authority to scope its own disqualification), the other serves every other layer and lists this one's declarations (reasoning by analogy from [R-ERR-04]'s narrowest-scope resource-decline pattern and from section 17.4's verifier treatment). The document decides between neither.
findings.quotation_a: There are no subset profiles: software that declines to support a core codec, a core filter, either channel layout, a core sample type, an assigned user-metadata encoding, or a registered record type is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It determines whether a real (if non-conforming) implementation's bytes for requests against the file's OTHER layers are served or withheld, and whether a layer-listing call includes the undecodable layer's name/declarations at all - a genuine behavioral fork with no textual tiebreaker, not merely a classification label.

findings.location_a: edition A: §6.2 trailer table (line 840); §6.3 [R-CNT-08] (lines 900-920); §10.1 vehicle list and [R-EXT-01] (lines 1580-1594); register row F19 (line 3882)
findings.title: Trailer's 16-bit 'incompat lane' can never be populated under this spec's own closed extension-vehicle list
findings.detail: The trailer's flags field is explicitly split into an 'incompat lane' (bits 0-15) and an 'ignore lane' (bits 16-31), a naming and position that, in every format this pattern is borrowed from, exists so a minor version can signal a feature old readers must reject rather than silently ignore. But section 10.1's closed, four-item list of the only ways this format grows names, as its sole trailer-flag vehicle, 'New ignore-lane flag bits' - never incompat-lane bits - and [R-EXT-01] closes the list ('Nothing else extends this format'). Every mention of the incompat lane in the document (seven places) describes it only as currently all-zero with any set bit always rejected (F19), never as something a minor-version vehicle can ever populate; and since [R-CNT-24] lets a future MAJOR version redefine the whole 48-byte trailer remainder anyway (flags field included), a future major does not need these specific 16 bits pre-reserved either. The practical upshot is that, under this document's own rules, bits 0-15 of the trailer flags are dead space for the entire life of format major 1 across every one of its minor versions, past and future - a lane named and positioned as if it had a job the document's own growth model never lets it do.
findings.quotation_a: This format grows through exactly four vehicles ... 3. New ignore-lane flag bits in the trailer (section 6.3) ... Nothing else extends this format.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Current conforming-reader behavior is already fully and unambiguously determined (F19: any incompat-lane bit set is reject-file, with no exception, forever, under this text) - resolving the observation would not change what bytes a reader accepts or rejects today. What it leaves undetermined is the document's own design intent and internal consistency in reserving a named, positioned lane that its own four-vehicle extension model never permits anything to use.

findings.title: Exact byte offsets of appended regions within one commit are writer-chosen, not fixed
findings.detail: The append procedure fixes the ordered sequence of high-level steps (payloads+indexes, then directory, then pad+trailer) and the overall step order, but the relative placement/offsets of a layer's new payload versus its new index region, and the interleaving of multiple changed layers' structures within one commit, are left to R-SLB-05's placement freedom whenever no alignment/slab is declared. An implementer building Probe W2's byte-offset table from the document alone cannot derive a single fixed set of offsets (only fixed sizes and a fixed high-level ordering) — two conforming appenders doing the identical logical edit will legitimately diverge in exact offsets, which is intentional per R-CNF-05/R-SLB-05 but worth flagging since it bounds how precise a 'byte layout' answer to W2 can be.
findings.quotation_a: Writers MUST NOT emit any other value ... That freedom is over *ordering and relative position*, and a byte the live state does not claim is slack whatever produced it (§5.2).
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It changes which exact bytes (offsets) a conforming appender may emit for the identical logical edit — two implementations will legitimately diverge in offsets though never in validity, which bears directly on how two implementers' byte-level walks of W2 could differ without either being wrong.

findings.title: Creator-vs-rewriter status is a self-declared position, not a function of what bytes a tool actually reproduces
findings.detail: A tool that reads an existing file and writes a new one can choose to be a 'creator' (flags=0, no preservation duty, answers for every byte including ones copied from the input) or a 'rewriter' (must preserve per §20.4/§20.5, carries forward unknown ignore-lane bits), and the document states this is the tool's own choice rather than something determined by how much of the input content it reproduces. Probe W5(c)'s answer (flags=0, dropping the ignore-lane bit) hinges entirely on this self-declared label even though the described operation (read input, decode, write new file) could, verbatim, also describe a rewrite that happens to re-create every layer. Two implementers building semantically similar 'read-and-regenerate' tools could legitimately produce different flags-handling behavior purely by labelling their own code path differently, with no byte-level test in the document to adjudicate which label a given tool actually is.
findings.quotation_a: A writer of a new file from an existing one takes one of two positions, and the choice is its own. As a rewriter it undertakes to preserve its input ... As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read: §20.2 binds it, it writes flags = 0 ... bytes it copied from another file included.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It directly changes the output trailer's flags byte (ignore-lane bits preserved vs. cleared) and the file_id provenance rule, for what can be an operationally identical input-to-output transformation, solely based on a self-declared, undefined-by-bytes 'position.'

findings.title: A barred fill-value change on a stored-tile layer is undetectable when the layer has no padding tiles
findings.detail: §20.3 bars a commit from changing a stored-tile layer's channel fill, but states explicitly that this writer-conduct bar does not by itself make a file nonconforming; the only detection mechanism the document names is T4 (`[R-SER-05]`), which checks that a padding position's bytes still encode the channel's current fill. Padding positions exist only in edge tiles where a dimension's extent does not divide its tile extent exactly (§11.3). For a layer whose every dimension's extent divides its tile extent exactly — a layer with no edge tiles at all — no padding position exists for any channel, so T4 (and every other register row) has nothing to check, and a conforming reader or verifier accepts the resulting file without exception. An implementation can therefore violate the fill-change bar and still produce a file every check in §21 certifies, with no trace distinguishing it from a file that never changed. A layer with dimension/tile-extent pairs that divide evenly (e.g. extent 256, tile extent 256: grid count 1, no overhang) stores a tile, then an appender's commit changes only that channel's declared fill value, leaving the stored tile's bytes untouched. The resulting file passes the trailer, directory, index-chain, and every T1-T26 register check; a conforming verifier certifies it. Two implementations given the same 'do not change fill' instruction thus diverge at the byte level — one emits the forbidden change, one does not — and nothing in the file distinguishes them nor does any check reject the one that violated the rule.
findings.quotation_a: "A commit MUST NOT change one of these; the change is a new layer, or a rewrite that re-declares it under a fresh file_id ... This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: This decides whether a conforming reader must accept a given byte sequence (post-fill-change, no-padding case) as fully valid — it must, by the document's own register, even though the writer action that produced it is explicitly forbidden conduct; an implementer relying on T4 to catch every fill-change violation would wrongly assume this case is also caught.

findings.title: Whether MU=1/PE=0 fixed by an implemented-but-unregistered type's own definition still forces no-drop retention is stated two ways
findings.detail: §7.2's Note states, apparently unconditionally, that `[R-CNT-12]` collapses every record into three states because 'MU = 1, whose PE bit is read as 1 whatever is stored' — tying that collapse directly to §20.4's three table rows with no carve-out. §20.4 itself, discussing a type the updater implements but this specification does not register, says the opposite for that case: 'the definition it implements the type from supplies the flags, and the stored bits never do ... so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites' — explicitly removing implemented types from the no-drop MU=1 row and letting PE=0 alone license a drop. For a record whose governing definition fixes MU=1 and PE=0, the two passages select different outcomes: the Note's logic would retain the record byte-identically with no drop permitted, while §20.4's explicit carve-out would let the updater drop it. An updater implements an unregistered record type X from a third-party specification that assigns X the flags MU=1, PE=0; in a commit that does not otherwise touch the scope X governs, it wants to drop a stale X record. One implementer reads 'so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites' and drops it (PE=0 licenses a drop); another reads the §7.2 Note's unconditional MU=1-collapses-PE-to-1 rule and retains it byte-identically, refusing to drop. Both implementers can point to an exact sentence for their behavior, and the two resulting files (one with the record present, one without) cannot both be the unique conforming output of the same commit, so at most one reading is the specification's intent, and the document does not say which.
findings.quotation_a: "[R-CNT-12] leaves a record three states, not four, and they are §20.4's three rows: MU = 1, whose PE bit is read as 1 whatever is stored" versus "Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement ... so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: This decides whether a conforming updater's commit that drops such a record (or, symmetrically, retains it) is the one the specification licenses — i.e., whether the record's bytes may legally be absent from, or must be present in, the next commit's directory. The two readings produce different, mutually exclusive sets of bytes a conforming updater may emit for the same input.

findings.title: Sec.2.4 labels every register outcome a 'reader outcome' without qualification; Sec.21.1 narrows this for verifier-only rows
findings.detail: Sec.2.4 states unqualified: every detectable violation 'is assigned exactly one reader outcome: reject-file, reject-layer, reject-tile, or ignore-record.' Over 3,000 lines later, Sec.21.1 narrows this for the ~20 rows whose Detector is verifier: 'the outcome names the scope at which the damage is recorded, not an obligation on any reader' -- for such rows a reader that serves the data unchanged is still conforming (Sec.21.1 names R-CNT-22 and R-MTA-05 as rows the reader 'serves ... unchanged'). An implementation built from Sec.2.4's definition and the register's bare Outcome column, without separately applying Sec.21.1's Detector-keyed carve-out, would wrongly refuse scopes (e.g. a layer whose only defect is L49, a stored-flags/registry mismatch) that this specification requires a conforming reader to serve.
findings.quotation_a: Every detectable file-conformance violation named by this specification is assigned exactly one **reader outcome**: reject-file, reject-layer, reject-tile, or ignore-record.
findings.quotation_b: For a row whose Detector is *verifier*, the outcome names the scope at which the damage is recorded, not an obligation on any reader.
findings.byte_level_rationale: A reader that treats every Outcome-column entry (including verifier-only rows like L49, F28, L46-L49, T2/T4/T5/T26) as its own refusal obligation would reject and fail to serve scopes this document requires a conforming reader to serve unchanged; a reader that correctly applies Sec.21.1's carve-out would serve them. That is a real difference in which bytes a conforming implementation returns for the same input file, turning on which of the two passages (read in isolation vs. together) governs the implementer's behavior.

findings.location_a: Sec.20.3 ('The line is drawn where a stored tile's meaning is fixed' paragraph)
findings.location_b: Sec.9.7 (note on not enumerating prior commits)
findings.title: A changed fixed declaration over a stored tile is, by the document's own consistent account, almost entirely unwitnessed
findings.detail: Probe V5 turns on this: the document states, in two separate sections that agree with each other, that (a) a verifier's walk never sees commit history at all, only the live state reached from the live trailer, so whether 'the last commit' changed anything is not a question any check asks; and (b) even within the one generation a verifier does see, the consequences of such a change are invisible except where they incidentally trip one of a named, closed set of other register rows (decoded-size/window/content-size/padding/pad-bit/boolean-byte/codec-framing rows T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2, T17, T24, T25). This is not a contradiction -- it is the document's own, repeated, and consistent description of its own detection boundary -- but it is the decisive, load-bearing fact behind answering V5, and worth recording plainly: a verifier implementation that tried to detect 'did an update change fixed declarations' as its own check would be building something this specification affirmatively does not provide.
findings.quotation_a: Under new [declarations] the same bytes would denote values, coordinates or padding the writer did not store, with every checksum in Sec.8 certifying the result and ... no check any actor owes able to see it (Sec.21.7).
findings.quotation_b: Nothing here enumerates prior commits. A verifier certifies what a reader can reach and counts what it cannot, which is decidable from the live trailer in one pass and does not depend on reconstructing the file's history.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Resolving this does not change what bytes a conforming implementation may emit, accept, or reject: the specification already fixes the answer unambiguously (no check sees the condition directly; only its incidental fallout through the named rules is caught), and two readers who each read the whole document would reach the identical implementation. I report it as an observation describing the decisive mechanism behind a probe answer, not as an unresolved question.

findings.location_a: section17.4 (Certification under codecs), first two sentences, read against R-CNF-03 in section2.3
findings.title: 'Cannot execute a codec' means different things for assigned vs unassigned codec values
findings.detail: section17.4's opening sentence makes 'cannot execute a layer's codec or filter' yield verdict cannot-establish, unqualified. Read alone this conflicts with R-CNF-03's 'no subset profiles: software that declines any of those [core codecs] is not a conforming reader' -- which would seem to disqualify such software outright rather than let it report cannot-establish. The very next sentence of section17.4 resolves this by confining the cannot-establish branch, for a conforming reader, to reserved/experimental codec values only (where it is in fact an ordinary L43/reject-layer violation, not a capability gap), leaving the 'genuinely cannot execute an assigned codec' case to describe non-conforming software's reporting discipline rather than a status a conforming verifier occupies for values 1-4. An implementer who quotes only the opening sentence (as a probe answer easily could) reaches a materially different, broader rule than the section as a whole states.
findings.quotation_a: A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file...For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer (R-COD-03, R-COD-09); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (R-CNF-03).
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Which reading is applied changes which verdict and which register row (L43/reject-layer vs. cannot-establish) a conforming verifier reports for the same stored codec-value bytes, i.e. changes what the certificate says for identical file content.

findings.location_a: section20.3 step4 (the fixed-declaration bar and its symptom list) read against section21.7's unwitnessed-condition test
findings.title: A bare name change on a layer that stored a tile is a writer violation no verifier can ever detect
findings.detail: section20.3 step4 bars a commit from changing certain 'fixed' declarations of a layer that stored a tile, but explicitly states this bar is writer-conduct only and 'no register row records the violation itself...the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit.' The section's own symptom list shows most instances of this bar (re-type, re-tile, codec/filter change) do incidentally surface through ordinary T-rows when the reinterpreted bytes break a content check -- but the document's own paradigm case, a bare name change (or two channel names swapped) on a layer that stored a tile, produces no such symptom at all ('a name enters no map this specification defines'). By section21.7's own test for 'unwitnessed,' this means a verifier built exactly to spec will certify such a file as conforming even though no conforming writer could have produced it, for this specific instance, with no detection path even in principle.
findings.quotation_a: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself...the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit (section21.7, R-ERR-01, R-CNF-02)...a name enters no map this specification defines, and a commit MAY change several names at once, two swapped included.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: For the bare name-swap instance specifically, no byte any conforming verifier emits, accepts, or rejects changes under either reading -- the document deliberately designs this case to be invisible to every check; the byte-level effect only reappears in the adjacent T-row-triggering instances, which are separately registered and not part of this finding's unwitnessed core.

findings.title: No stated priority among §6.2's grouped post-gate trailer checks
findings.detail: §6.2 states a strict sequence for exactly three gates (trailer magic, trailer CRC, version gate) and then introduces a distinct, larger set of checks — the flag gates, committed_file_length equality and multiple-of-64, dir_offset >= 16, dir_length >= 4, the offset+length bound, file_id != 0, reserved bytes all zero — under the heading 'the reader MUST validate all of the following,' with no ordering language among that group's own members. Every member independently yields reject-file, so the outcome class for a file failing several of them at once is unaffected, but which specific diagnostic (e.g. 'bad file_id' vs 'reserved bytes nonzero') a reader is to surface first when two or more of that group's conditions fail on the same file is not fixed by the text. I found this while testing, then discarding, a quiz question that would have asked 'which check is reported first' for a file failing two of these simultaneously; I could not derive a single determinate answer and dropped the question rather than force one.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST validate, in order: the trailer magic; the trailer CRC; the version gate (§6.3)... If those gates pass, the reader MUST validate all of the following before acting on the fields involved: the flag gates (§6.3); committed_file_length equals the file size...; dir_offset ≥ 16; dir_length ≥ 4; dir_offset + dir_length ≤ F − 64...; file_id ≠ 0; reserved bytes all zero. Any failure is reject-file.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is an internal-consistency observation about a single edition (B), not a two-edition comparison, so there is no byte or verdict in a second text to compare against; no quotation_b or location_b applies. It concerns diagnostic-reporting order among several reader checks that all share one outcome class, not a disputed byte value.

result.notes: Summary under the implementer-consequence lens: across all 29 reported findings, grouped into 17 distinct differences/defects, none produces a byte-level divergence between an implementation built from edition B alone and one built from edition A alone — byte_level is false for every group, so byte_level_count is 0. Roughly half the raw findings (cod11-reader-capability-gap, incompat-lane-never-populated, reader-outcome-unqualified-vs-verifier-detector-carveout, fixed-declaration-change-unwitnessed, mu1-pe0-note-vs-20.4-table, writer-chosen-append-offsets, creator-rewriter-self-declared, trailer-post-gate-check-order) turned out, on direct comparison of both editions, to rest on text that is unchanged between A and B — these are single-edition drafting ambiguities/observations (some real, one a straightforward misreading in R-COD-11's case, one resolved by reading the full Note sentence in the MU=1/PE=0 case) rather than fidelity differences, and I graded them EQUIVALENT or REPORTER_ERROR accordingly rather than passing them through as unresolved AMBIGUITY, per the four-way consensus scale this round uses. The remaining findings split into confirmed, genuine LOSSes (six groups: §3.3's independence note, the F14/F5/F15 reach-derivation Note, the §2.4 reject-scope Note, the R-ENC-08 scope Note, the relocated negative carve-out on experimental-range metadata, and the MU=1-unimplemented/experimental derivation clause — all verified by direct quotation of both editions plus a control grep proving absence in B) and two confirmed ADDITIONs (the new §15.4 Rationale figures and the §16.2 Note→Rationale expansion), both of which the repository's own commit log shows were intentional, maintainer-reviewed edits. Every one of the six LOSSes is non-normative explanatory material (a Note, Rationale, or derivation clause carrying no requirement ID of its own) whose removal leaves the governing rule, register row, or table it explained unchanged and still fully decisive — so while real and worth repairing for a reader trying to understand or extend the spec, none of them changes what a conforming implementation accepts, rejects, or emits today. I verified every claimed absence with a positive-control grep (confirming the search mechanism works on known-present text) before counting it as a genuine zero, per the brief's instruction on hard-wrapped prose.

result.decisive_quotes:
R-CNF-01, identical verbatim in both editions (A:105-107, B:156-158): "All text in this document is normative except: §1 (Introduction); any text labeled *Note*, *Example*, or *Rationale*; and appendices identified as non-normative. `[R-CNF-01]`"

A's Note (A:2421-2431): "**Note — what slabs are, and are not.** A slab guarantees *contiguity*: consecutive disk ordinals occupy consecutive bytes. Which tiles are ordinal-consecutive is the linearization field's job (§11.4); under row-major, a run is a band along the last-declared dimension. Rectangular-window locality is therefore not a slab property — it belongs to the reserved space-filling-curve linearization values, under which the same slab machinery, unchanged, would make compact windows contiguous. Slabs are the byte-layout half of that future answer. With A_slab = 1 a slab is contiguity-only — the right declaration for remote range coalescing with no direct-I/O alignment need."

B's Rationale (B:2301-2319): "**Rationale.** A slab promises one thing, contiguity: within a run, consecutive disk ordinals occupy consecutive bytes. A reader that wants a run can therefore fetch it as one range, however many tiles it holds and whatever their stored sizes, and a planner can size a buffer and issue one direct read per run before it has fetched a single index byte. A reader holding the index entries can always detect contiguity by arithmetic; what the declaration adds is the promise in advance, checkable by a verifier, with the index left as it is, one entry per tile. Which tiles are consecutive in ordinal is not the slab's business but the linearization field's (§11.4): under row-major, a run is a band along the last-declared dimension. So a slab does not by itself make a rectangular window contiguous; that locality belongs to the reserved space-filling-curve linearization values, under which the same slab machinery, unchanged, would make compact windows contiguous. Slabs are the byte-layout half of that future answer. A_slab adds alignment for direct I/O at each run's start; with A_slab = 1 a slab is contiguity alone, the right declaration for coalescing remote range requests when no direct-I/O alignment is needed."

A's §16.1 Note, byte-identical in substance to B's (A:2362-2365 / B:2245-2248), establishing the direct-I/O role of alignment that B's Rationale draws on by analogy for A_slab: "**Note.** 4096 — the page size and modern physical sector size — is the recommended value for writers that align: it satisfies O_DIRECT, mmap, and GPU direct-storage paths everywhere. 512 is the legacy sector floor."

Governing rule R-SLB-03, substantively unchanged (A:2395-2398 / B:2277-2279): A: "A verifier MUST check these invariants (violation: reject-layer, §15.3); readers are not obligated to, and MAY instead detect contiguity arithmetically from any index segment. `[R-SLB-03]`" — B: "A verifier MUST check these invariants (violation: reject-layer, §15.3); readers are not obligated to, and MAY instead detect contiguity arithmetically from any index segment. `[R-SLB-03]`" (verbatim identical).
result.reasoning:
The group's claim is a label change (Note → Rationale) plus added explanatory sentences in §16.2's third blockquote. To refute the triage's dismissal I needed either (a) a LOSS — some rule, carve-out or quantifier A states that B now states only inside a non-normative block (or narrower/wider), or (b) an ADDITION that survives the byte-level test — B deciding something A leaves open in a way that would make a conforming implementation built from B alone emit different bytes or reach a different accept/reject verdict than one built from A alone.

(a) is foreclosed immediately: R-CNF-01 — the rule that defines what counts as normative — is word-for-word identical in both editions (confirmed by exact grep match at A:105-107 and B:156-158, and by a control search confirming the defining sentence appears exactly once in each file). Under that identical rule, Note and Rationale are equally non-normative. So the content wasn't normative in A and demoted to non-normative in B; it was already non-normative in A, and remains non-normative in B. No rule, carve-out, exception, quantifier or definition migrates out of normative force by this relabelling, because it was never in normative force to begin with.

For (b), I checked the actual governing paragraphs of §16.2 — R-SLB-02 (run partitioning), R-SLB-03 (the contiguity/alignment/packing invariants and verifier obligation), and R-SLB-04 (the writer/updater re-establishment-or-clear obligation) — line by line between editions. The differences are exclusively punctuation and sentence-boundary reflow (e.g. a semicolon/dash replaced by a comma, one sentence split into two); no scope, quantifier, or condition changes. The two unlabelled "Note." blocks immediately before the renamed block, and the Example block after it, are also substantively identical (I verified every figure in the worked example: grid 4×8, N=32, S=8, A_slab=4096, four runs, the viewport spanning ordinals 8–23, and the sentinel-at-ordinal-10 case, all match exactly).

That leaves the added prose itself as the only candidate for an ADDITION with teeth. Three new claims appear in B that aren't in A's Note: (1) a run can be fetched "as one range... before it has fetched a single index byte" and used for buffer sizing; (2) a restatement that a reader can always detect contiguity by arithmetic, with the declaration adding only an advance, verifier-checkable promise; (3) an explicit statement that A_slab's purpose is "alignment for direct I/O at each run's start." For (3), I confirmed this is a fair derivation from A's own text, not manufactured: §16.1's Note (byte-identical in both editions) already states that per-tile alignment A "satisfies O_DIRECT, mmap, and GPU direct-storage paths," and §16.2's normative text in both editions calls A_slab "mutually exclusive with per-tile alignment" — establishing the analogy A makes only by implication ("the right declaration for remote range coalescing with no direct-I/O alignment need" implies, by contrast, that a positive A_slab choice serves direct-I/O need). (1) and (2) are elaborations of the single guarantee A already states ("contiguity: consecutive disk ordinals occupy consecutive bytes" necessarily implies fetchability as one range); the "before it has fetched a single index byte" clause is rhetorically loose (a reader still needs at least the run's first-tile offset from the index to issue a directed read) but it appears inside a block that is non-normative in both editions, so even if read literally it cannot alter what a writer, reader, or verifier is required to do, and therefore cannot change any byte emitted or any accept/reject verdict reached.

I deliberately checked for exactly the trap the brief warns about (Calibration 2's error): a difference elsewhere in the same paragraph that belongs to a different group. I found none in this passage — every sentence of both blocks traces to the same claim under review.

Given R-CNF-01 is identical, the governing R-SLB-02..05 rules are unchanged in substance, and the added sentences either derive fairly from A's own text or sit inside a block whose non-normative status is unchanged, the byte-level test comes back negative: no implementation built from B's normative text alone would emit different bytes or reach a different verdict than one built from A's. The triage's conclusion holds.
